laws.title: Handheld Phone Ban While Driving
laws.subtitle: CA Vehicle Code §23123 — Hands-free required
laws.fullDescription: Using any handheld mobile device while driving is illegal in California. Hands-free (Bluetooth, speakerphone on mount) is permitted. Applies at red lights too.
laws.penalty: 1st offense: $162. 2nd+: $285. No DMV points added.
exceptions: Emergency 911 calls
Law enforcement on duty
Parked off roadway

quiz.q: Fine for first handheld phone offense in California?
quiz.explanation: First offense is $162 including penalty assessments.

laws.title: Smoking Restrictions in Public Places
laws.subtitle: CA Health & Safety Code §118920 — 25ft from doorways
laws.fullDescription: Smoking prohibited in all enclosed workplaces, within 25 feet of doorways/windows of public buildings, state parks, many beaches, near playgrounds.
laws.penalty: $100 first violation, up to $500 subsequent. Business owners face additional fines.
exceptions: Private residences
Designated outdoor smoking areas
Licensed tobacco retailers

quiz.q: Required distance from building doorways to smoke in California?
quiz.explanation: California requires 25 feet clearance from doorways, windows and ventilation systems.

laws.title: Rent Control — AB 1482 Tenant Protection
laws.subtitle: Caps annual increases at 5% + CPI or 10% max
laws.fullDescription: Under AB 1482 (Tenant Protection Act 2019), most landlords can only raise rent by 5% + local inflation or 10% — whichever is lower. Applies to housing 15+ years old.
laws.penalty: Landlords face civil liability, repayment of illegal increases plus interest.
exceptions: Single-family homes with proper notice
Buildings under 15 years old
Condos sold separately

quiz.q: Maximum annual rent increase under California AB 1482?
quiz.explanation: Capped at 5% + local CPI or 10%, whichever is lower.

laws.title: Jaywalking — Freedom to Walk Act
laws.subtitle: AB 2147 (2023) — Decriminalized unless immediate danger
laws.fullDescription: As of Jan 2023, jaywalking is decriminalized. You can cross outside crosswalks when safe. Citations only if there is 'immediate danger of collision.'
laws.penalty: Citation only if immediate danger: $197 fine.
exceptions: Must yield to vehicles
Cannot cross during immediate danger

quiz.q: Under CA's Freedom to Walk Act, when can you still be cited?
options: When there is immediate danger of collision
quiz.explanation: Jaywalking is only citable when there is 'immediate danger of collision.'

laws.title: Minimum Wage — $16.90/hour
laws.subtitle: Statewide rate effective January 1, 2026
laws.fullDescription: California's statewide minimum wage is $16.90 per hour for all employers as of January 1, 2026. Fast-food restaurant employers have had a higher minimum wage since April 1, 2024. Some healthcare employers, and some cities and counties, set a higher rate.
laws.penalty: Back wages, $100–$250 per violation per employee, civil lawsuits.
exceptions: Some apprenticeship programs
Outside sales employees

quiz.q: California state minimum wage as of January 2024?
quiz.explanation: California minimum wage is $16.00/hour statewide from Jan 1, 2024.

laws.title: California Social Culture — Laid-back & First-name
laws.subtitle: Informal, wellness-focused, environmentally conscious
laws.fullDescription: Californians are typically casual and friendly. First names are used immediately in almost all contexts. Environmental consciousness is highly valued — commenting positively on eco-friendly choices earns respect. LA culture prizes wellness and outdoor activity. San Francisco tech culture is very direct and values disruption and innovation.
laws.penalty: No legal penalty — social friction from being overly formal or dismissive of environmental issues.
exceptions: Formal legal and government settings use titles
Hollywood/entertainment industry has its own unique hierarchy

quiz.q: What social value is particularly important in California culture?
quiz.explanation: Environmental consciousness and sustainability are deeply valued in California culture.

laws.title: FinCEN $10,000 Currency Declaration — Applies to Every US Entry/Exit
laws.subtitle: 31 USC §5316 (FBAR/CMIR) — Undeclared currency forfeiture + criminal charges
laws.fullDescription: Anyone entering or leaving the United States with more than USD $10,000 (or its equivalent in any currency, monetary instruments, gold coins, or negotiable instruments) must file a FinCEN Form 105 — the Currency or Monetary Instrument Report (CMIR) — with US Customs and Border Protection. The threshold applies to families travelling together (aggregated), not just individuals. Failure to declare means automatic forfeiture of the full amount — even if the money is entirely legitimate — and exposes the traveller to criminal prosecution under 31 USC §5322. CBP officers do ask the $10,000 question during primary inspection and accept the answer under oath; lying is a separate felony (18 USC §1001). Forfeited amounts do not require a criminal conviction to be kept by the government. This rule applies equally on departure and arrival, and applies on every US border (including land crossings to Canada and Mexico). California’s major international airports (LAX, SFO) and border crossings see frequent cases.
laws.penalty: Failure to declare: forfeiture of entire amount + civil fine up to the amount carried. Wilful false statement or structuring: up to 5 years imprisonment + $500,000 fine under 31 USC §5322 and 18 USC §1001.
exceptions: Amounts under $10,000 aggregate per family travelling together
Diplomatic couriers holding valid Department of State credentials

quiz.q: When entering the USA with more than $10,000, which form must a traveller file with CBP?
quiz.explanation: The Currency or Monetary Instrument Report (FinCEN Form 105 / CMIR) must be filed with CBP for any amount over $10,000 per family. Failure to declare triggers automatic forfeiture.

laws.title: Wildfire Rules — Campfire Bans, Red Flag Warnings and Defensible Space Law
laws.subtitle: PRC §4291 — 100ft defensible space mandatory; campfire bans strictly enforced
laws.fullDescription: California experiences the most destructive wildfires in US history — the 2018 Camp Fire killed 85 people and destroyed Paradise. California's Public Resources Code §4291 requires all homes within State Responsibility Areas (SRAs) to maintain 100 feet of 'defensible space' by clearing brush and combustible materials. During Red Flag Warning conditions (issued by the National Weather Service), campfire bans apply throughout State and National Forests — violations carry criminal charges. Starting a wildfire through negligence in California can result in state suppression cost billing of millions of dollars and criminal prosecution. Fireworks are banned year-round in many California cities.
laws.penalty: Violating campfire ban: $1,000 fine + criminal misdemeanor. Negligently starting a wildfire: liable for all suppression costs + criminal charges. Illegal fireworks: $50,000 fine.
exceptions: Propane and gas stoves are generally allowed even during campfire bans
Prescribed burns by CAL FIRE with permits
laws.sourceLabel: CAL FIRE — Campfire and Fire Restrictions

quiz.q: Under California Public Resources Code §4291, how many feet of defensible space must homeowners in State Responsibility Areas maintain?
quiz.explanation: California's PRC §4291 requires 100 feet of defensible space around homes in State Responsibility Areas — clearing brush, trees, and combustible materials in a two-zone system to reduce wildfire risk.

laws.title: California Vehicle Emissions — CARB Standards and Zero-Emission Mandates
laws.subtitle: CARB 2035 mandate — No new petrol-only cars by 2035; strictest US standards
laws.fullDescription: California's Air Resources Board (CARB) sets the strictest vehicle emissions standards in the USA — and 17 other states have adopted California's standards under the Clean Air Act Section 177. California passed a rule requiring all new passenger cars sold in California by 2035 to be zero-emission (electric, hydrogen, or plug-in hybrid). Older diesel vehicles face restrictions in many cities: Sacramento's Clean Air Zone and similar low-emission zones restrict heavy diesel vehicles. The Smog Check programme requires biennial emissions testing for most vehicles. Vehicles registered in other states must comply with California standards within a year of becoming California residents. Electric vehicle (EV) rebates and HOV (carpool) lane access are significant incentives.
laws.penalty: Selling a new non-compliant vehicle after 2035 deadline: CARB fine up to $50,000 per vehicle. Failed smog check: vehicle may not be legally registered.
exceptions: True zero-emission vehicles (EVs, fuel cell) are exempt from smog checks
Off-road and farm equipment have separate (less strict) standards
laws.sourceLabel: California Air Resources Board — Zero-Emission Vehicle Regulations

quiz.q: By what year must all new passenger cars sold in California be zero-emission vehicles?
quiz.explanation: California's Air Resources Board (CARB) mandated that all new passenger cars and light trucks sold in California must be zero-emission by 2035 — the most ambitious such mandate in the USA, influencing similar rules in 17 other states and internationally.

laws.title: California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) — Strongest US State Privacy Law
laws.subtitle: CCPA gives Californians rights to know, delete, and opt out of sale of personal data
laws.fullDescription: The California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA, 2018, effective 2020) and its strengthening amendment the California Privacy Rights Act (CPRA, 2020, effective 2023) create the strongest consumer data privacy rights in the United States. Key rights: know what data is collected, request deletion, opt out of sale/sharing of personal data, and correct inaccurate information. Businesses with over $25M revenue, or handling data of 100,000+ consumers, or deriving 50%+ revenue from data sales must comply. The California Privacy Protection Agency (CPPA) enforces violations. CCPA has functionally become the de facto national US privacy standard because multinationals find it easier to apply California rules universally than to geo-restrict. It applies to data of California residents globally — not just within California.
laws.penalty: Intentional CCPA violations: fines up to $7,500 per record. Unintentional violations: $2,500 per record. Data breach involving children's data: $7,500 per record. Private right of action for data breaches: $100–$750 per consumer.
exceptions: Businesses below the revenue/data thresholds are exempt
Employee HR data had a delayed exemption (expired 2023)
Nonprofit organizations meeting size threshold still have some exemptions
laws.sourceLabel: California Privacy Protection Agency — CCPA/CPRA Regulations

quiz.q: Why has California's CCPA functionally become a de facto national privacy standard in the USA?
options: The federal government adopted CCPA as federal law in 2021
Multinationals find it easier to apply California rules universally than geo-restrict by state
CCPA applies to all US residents, not just Californians
The Supreme Court ruled CCPA must apply nationwide
quiz.explanation: California's CCPA has become a de facto national standard because large companies find it operationally simpler to apply CCPA's privacy requirements to all their US customers rather than building systems to treat California residents differently — effectively giving all Americans CCPA-level protections.

laws.title: California's Three Strikes Law — Mandatory Life Sentences Reformed After Mass Incarceration Critique
laws.subtitle: California's 1994 Three Strikes law sent thousands to life for minor third offenses; 2012 reform narrowed it
laws.fullDescription: California's Three Strikes and You're Out law (1994) mandated 25-years-to-life imprisonment for any felony conviction if the defendant had two prior serious/violent felony convictions ('strikes') — including some minor third felonies. By 2012, California had 40,000+ three-strikes inmates, many for non-violent third offenses (petty theft, drug possession). Proposition 36 (2012) reformed the law: the mandatory 25-to-life sentence now only applies if the third strike is also serious or violent. An estimated 3,000 inmates serving life for non-violent third offenses became eligible for resentencing. California spends $81,000+ per year per inmate. The Three Strikes law reform represented a major shift in 'tough on crime' sentencing philosophy.
laws.penalty: Under reformed Three Strikes: 25-to-life only if third strike is serious/violent felony. Second strike (one prior): doubled sentence. First-time felonies: standard sentencing.
exceptions: Certain sex crimes against children retain mandatory life sentences regardless of reform
Murder, rape, and other specified crimes cannot be reclassified for resentencing
Federal three-strikes (Armed Career Criminal Act) has separate rules
laws.sourceLabel: California Legislature — Three Strikes Reform Proposition 36

quiz.q: What did California's 2012 Proposition 36 reform change about the Three Strikes law?
options: It completely abolished the Three Strikes law
The mandatory 25-to-life sentence now only applies if the third strike is also a serious or violent felony
It reduced all Three Strikes sentences to maximum 15 years
It transferred Three Strikes cases from state to federal courts
quiz.explanation: California's 2012 Proposition 36 narrowed Three Strikes so the mandatory 25-years-to-life sentence only applies when the third strike is also a serious or violent felony. Previously, even minor non-violent felonies as a third strike triggered automatic life sentences — a system that contributed to mass incarceration of people serving life for petty theft or minor drug offenses.

laws.title: Reparations Task Force for African Americans
laws.subtitle: California's reparations study became the most comprehensive in US history
laws.fullDescription: California's AB 3121 (2020) created a first-in-the-nation Task Force to Study and Develop Reparation Proposals for African Americans. The task force's 2023 final report recommended wide-ranging reparations: cash payments of up to $1.2 million per eligible person, elimination of medical debt for Black Californians, housing vouchers, free college tuition, and business grants — totaling an estimated $800 billion. Governor Newsom signed several non-cash reparations measures in 2024 (education, health, business programs) but declined cash payments, citing cost. The legislation sparked national debate about the practicality and justice of reparations.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties involved; task force recommendations are advisory. Legislative action required to implement any payments.
exceptions: Task force defined eligibility as descendants of enslaved African Americans in the US before 1900
California was a free state but the report documented how California policies harmed Black residents
Other localities including San Francisco developed their own separate reparations proposals

quiz.q: What was the estimated total cost of cash reparations recommended by California's 2023 reparations task force report?
quiz.explanation: California's reparations task force estimated its full recommendations — including cash payments of up to $1.2 million per eligible person — would cost approximately $800 billion, making it the most comprehensive reparations study in U.S. history.

laws.title: Proposition 47 Reform & Retail Theft Backlash
laws.subtitle: California's 2014 criminal justice reform was blamed for retail theft surge — voters partially reversed it in 2024
laws.fullDescription: California's Proposition 47 (2014) reclassified non-violent felonies as misdemeanors: drug possession, theft under $950, and forgery. The reforms were intended to reduce mass incarceration and redirect savings to mental health and substance abuse programs. However, as retail theft increased in 2021–2023 — with organized 'smash-and-grab' rings targeting luxury stores — critics blamed Prop 47's $950 threshold for enabling theft without meaningful consequences. Proposition 36 on the November 2024 ballot — backed by retailers including Target and Home Depot — passed with 68% of votes, allowing felony charges for repeat theft and drug offenders even below $950 and reinstating some prison sentences.
laws.penalty: Post-Prop 36 (2024): third repeat theft offense can be charged as felony regardless of amount. Drug possession with a prior: enhanced charges available. Organized retail crime: felony with up to 3 years per offense.
exceptions: First and second offense theft under $950 remains misdemeanor
Mental health diversion programs remain available as alternatives to prosecution
Prop 47 sentencing reductions for people already convicted remain in place

quiz.q: What dollar threshold for theft did California's Proposition 47 set that critics blamed for enabling retail theft?
quiz.explanation: Proposition 47 reclassified theft of goods under $950 as a misdemeanor rather than a felony — a threshold critics blamed when organized retail theft surged in 2021–2023, ultimately leading California voters to partially reverse the reform with Proposition 36 in 2024.

laws.title: California Net Neutrality Law (SB 822)
laws.subtitle: California passed the strongest net neutrality law in the US after the FCC repealed federal protections in 2017
laws.fullDescription: After the Federal Communications Commission repealed Obama-era net neutrality rules in 2017, California passed SB 822 (signed 2018) — widely regarded as the nation's strongest net neutrality law. It prohibits internet service providers from blocking or throttling legal content, creating paid fast lanes, or engaging in zero-rating (exempting certain apps from data caps to favor affiliated services). AT&T and other ISPs sued to block the law, and the Department of Justice joined the lawsuit. A federal court upheld California's law in 2021, and it fully took effect after the Biden administration restored federal net neutrality rules (later again challenged). California's law goes further than federal rules.
laws.penalty: Violations subject ISPs to enforcement by the California Attorney General; civil penalties up to $25,000 per violation per day
exceptions: Reasonable network management practices for congestion control are permitted
Enterprise services and private networks have different treatment

quiz.q: What is 'zero-rating,' which California's net neutrality law prohibits?
options: Exempting certain apps from data caps to favor affiliated services
quiz.explanation: Zero-rating means exempting certain apps or services from counting against data caps — effectively favoring the ISP's own services or paid partners over competitors, which California's SB 822 prohibits.

laws.title: California Reparations Task Force: America's Most Advanced Slavery Reparations Study
laws.subtitle: California created the most comprehensive US reparations study ever — recommending payments of up to $1.2 million per eligible Black Californian
laws.fullDescription: In 2020, California established the nation's first state-level Reparations Task Force to study and develop reparations proposals for African Americans. The Task Force's 2023 final report recommended cash payments of up to approximately $1.2 million per eligible Black Californian (based on lineage back to enslaved people and duration of California residence), plus agency-specific programs covering housing, education, healthcare, and business support. Total cost estimates ranged from $500 billion to over $800 billion. Governor Newsom signed several race-specific remediation bills while declining to immediately implement direct payments. California became a national flashpoint for the reparations debate, though California was never a slave state.
laws.penalty: No penalties — this is a policy proposal. Discriminatory implementation of any resulting programs would be subject to equal protection challenges
exceptions: Eligibility would be limited to those who can document descent from enslaved African Americans or free Black people living in the US before 1900
California's reparations discussion is separate from federal reparations proposals (HR 40) pending in Congress
laws.sourceLabel: California Office of Planning and Research – Reparations

quiz.q: Why is California's reparations proposal notable even though California was never a slave state?
options: California had the most escaped slaves
California profited from slavery through cotton trade
California's large Black population and historical discrimination still justify redress
quiz.explanation: California's Reparations Task Force argued that even though California was never a slave state, Black Californians experienced documented racial harms including housing discrimination, redlining, over-policing, and exclusion from wealth-building programs — justifying state-level reparations independent of the slavery question.

laws.title: CCPA Privacy Rights
laws.subtitle: California Consumer Privacy Act gives residents sweeping data control
laws.fullDescription: The California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA), effective January 2020 and strengthened by the California Privacy Rights Act (CPRA) in 2023, gives California residents the right to know what personal data businesses collect about them, the right to delete it, the right to opt out of its sale, and the right to non-discrimination for exercising these rights. Businesses with over $25M revenue, or those that handle data of 100,000+ consumers, must comply. The California Privacy Protection Agency (CPPA) enforces the law with fines up to $7,500 per intentional violation. CCPA has become a de facto national privacy standard as many companies apply it across the US.
laws.penalty: $2,500 per unintentional violation, $7,500 per intentional violation; private right of action for data breaches ($100–$750 per consumer
exceptions: Small businesses below revenue and data thresholds are exempt
Employee data and B2B data had temporary exemptions, now removed under CPRA

quiz.q: What is the maximum fine per intentional CCPA violation?
quiz.explanation: The CCPA/CPRA allows the California Privacy Protection Agency to fine businesses $7,500 per intentional violation of consumer privacy rights.

laws.title: Coastal Act
laws.subtitle: California's Coastal Act protects public beach access and coastal development
laws.fullDescription: California's Coastal Act (1976) established the California Coastal Commission, which has authority over all development within the 'coastal zone' — roughly 1,100 miles of coastline extending inland from 1,000 yards to 5 miles depending on terrain. All development (including home renovations) requires a Coastal Development Permit. The Act mandates that public access to beaches cannot be blocked — private landowners cannot legally prevent people from accessing the ocean below the mean high tide line. The Commission famously denied permits to illegal staircase removal and private beach exclusions, including a high-profile battle with Vinod Khosla (venture capitalist) over Martins Beach access.
laws.penalty: Unpermitted development in the coastal zone: cease-and-desist orders, fines up to $15,000 per day, and mandatory restoration
exceptions: Emergency repair of existing structures may proceed before permit approval
Agricultural operations with minimal coastal impact may be exempt

quiz.q: What principle about beach access does California's Coastal Act protect?
options: All beaches must be free of charge
No private development within 100 feet of the ocean
The public cannot be blocked from accessing beaches below the mean high tide line
quiz.explanation: California's Coastal Act protects the public's right to access the ocean — private landowners cannot block access to beaches below the mean high tide line. This has been enforced in high-profile cases against wealthy landowners who tried to privatize beach access.

laws.title: AB5 Gig Worker Law
laws.subtitle: California's AB5 reclassified gig workers as employees — then was partly reversed
laws.fullDescription: California Assembly Bill 5 (AB5, 2019) applied the 'ABC test' to determine worker classification — requiring companies to treat workers as employees (not independent contractors) unless they meet strict conditions (A: free from company control, B: do work outside company's usual business, C: independently established in that trade). AB5 specifically targeted ride-share companies (Uber, Lyft) and delivery apps. Uber and Lyft funded Proposition 22 (2020), spending $200 million to pass a ballot measure exempting app-based gig workers from AB5. The Prop 22 exemption was challenged in court — ultimately upheld in 2023. AB5 still applies to most other industries.
laws.penalty: Misclassifying employees as contractors: back payroll taxes, benefits, fines; civil penalties; criminal charges for systematic violations
exceptions: Proposition 22 exempts app-based transportation and delivery workers
Many professions (lawyers, doctors, licensed contractors) are exempt by statute

quiz.q: How much did Uber and Lyft spend to pass Proposition 22 (the AB5 gig worker exemption) in 2020?
quiz.explanation: Uber, Lyft, DoorDash, Instacart, and other app-based companies spent approximately $200 million on Proposition 22 — the most expensive ballot initiative in California history — to exempt themselves from AB5's employee classification requirements.

laws.title: AB 5 Gig Worker Law and Proposition 22
laws.subtitle: California's worker classification battle between gig companies and employees reshaped labor law
laws.fullDescription: California's Assembly Bill 5 (AB 5, effective January 1, 2020) codified the 'ABC test' from the Dynamex California Supreme Court ruling (2018) to determine worker classification. Under the ABC test, workers are presumed employees (not independent contractors) unless the company can prove: (A) the worker is free from the company's control and direction; (B) the work is outside the company's usual business; and (C) the worker is customarily engaged in an independently established trade. This effectively classified most Uber, Lyft, and DoorDash drivers as employees entitled to minimum wage, overtime, and benefits. Gig companies spent $200 million to pass Proposition 22 in November 2020, creating a special category for app-based delivery/ride companies that allowed them to keep drivers as contractors with limited new benefits. Prop 22 was initially struck down by a Alameda County judge in 2021 but upheld by the Court of Appeal in 2023.
laws.penalty: Misclassifying employees as contractors under AB 5: back wages, penalties of $5,000–$25,000 per violation, and class action liability
exceptions: Proposition 22 exempts app-based transportation/delivery companies that meet its standards
Over 100 occupation exemptions were added to AB 5 (doctors, lawyers, licensed tradespeople, certain freelancers)
Business-to-business relationships may be exempt if meeting specific criteria

laws.title: AI Safety Bill SB 1047 and California AI Regulation
laws.subtitle: California's 2024 AI safety bill was vetoed but sparked the global AI governance debate
laws.fullDescription: California Senate Bill 1047 (SB 1047, 2024), authored by Senator Scott Wiener, was a landmark attempt to regulate the development of advanced AI systems. The bill would have required developers of AI models costing over $100 million to train to: implement safety protocols and 'kill switches' to shut down AI systems; conduct safety testing before deployment; maintain records of training and capabilities; and establish whistleblower protections for AI safety researchers. SB 1047 received significant support from some AI safety researchers (including many at Anthropic, who publicly debated it) but opposition from major tech companies (OpenAI, Google, Meta) and Governor Gavin Newsom's administration, who argued it would stifle AI innovation in California. Newsom vetoed the bill in September 2024, calling it 'well-intentioned but an ill-conceived approach.' California subsequently enacted lighter-touch bills: SB 942 (AI transparency disclosures), AB 2013 (training data disclosure), and others.
laws.penalty: Had SB 1047 passed: violations of safety protocols would carry civil liability; attorney general enforcement; operators of non-compliant systems would face injunctions. As vetoed: existing law applies
exceptions: Open-source AI models had contested exemptions in the bill's various amendments
Academic research had reduced requirements
Government AI systems had separate provisions

laws.title: California Reparations Task Force Recommendations
laws.subtitle: California studied reparations for African Americans descended from enslaved people
laws.fullDescription: In 2020, California established the nation's first state-level Reparations Task Force under AB 3121 to study reparations for African Americans, particularly those descended from enslaved people or free Black people living in the US before the end of the 19th century. The task force issued a final report in 2023 recommending direct payments, educational investments, business grants, and policy reforms. Governor Newsom signed several bills in 2024 implementing non-monetary reparations (formal apologies, history curricula), but declined to support direct cash payments. The effort highlighted California's unique history — it entered the Union as a free state but had Black codes and discriminatory laws.
laws.penalty: Discriminatory lending practices: civil suits up to $250,000 under Unruh Civil Rights Act. Redlining violations: federal Fair Housing Act penalties.
exceptions: Reparations eligibility criteria debated and not yet finalized
Non-monetary measures (apologies, curriculum) implemented separately from cash proposals

quiz.q: What did California's 2023 Reparations Task Force recommend?
options: Immediate $1M payments to all Black Californians
Direct payments, educational investments, and policy reforms for eligible African Americans
A constitutional amendment banning racial discrimination
Mandatory diversity quotas in state government
quiz.explanation: The task force recommended direct payments, business grants, educational investments, and other reforms targeting African Americans descended from enslaved people or free Black people pre-1900.

laws.title: SB 1047 – AI Safety Bill Vetoed by Governor Newsom
laws.subtitle: California's landmark AI safety bill was rejected, sparking national debate
laws.fullDescription: California's SB 1047 (Safe and Secure Innovation for Frontier Artificial Intelligence Models Act) would have required AI developers to implement safety protocols, conduct testing before deploying powerful AI models, and face civil liability for harms caused by their AI systems. It passed the legislature but was vetoed by Governor Gavin Newsom in September 2024, who argued it was too broad and would drive AI companies out of California. The veto was celebrated by major tech companies including OpenAI, Google, and Meta, but condemned by AI safety advocates. Newsom signed several narrower AI bills instead. The debate over AI regulation — federal vs. state, broad vs. targeted — intensified nationally.
laws.penalty: Under vetoed SB 1047: civil liability for AI harms. Alternative signed bills: fines for AI deepfake election interference, disclosure requirements for AI-generated content.
exceptions: Open-source AI models had modified requirements under SB 1047
Research and development activities given extended timelines

quiz.q: Why did Governor Newsom veto California's SB 1047 AI safety bill?
options: He argued it would violate the US Constitution's commerce clause
He said it was too broad and would drive AI companies out of California
He preferred a federal approach and wanted Congress to act first
The bill had insufficient penalties to deter violations
quiz.explanation: Newsom vetoed SB 1047 arguing it was overly broad and would harm California's AI industry and innovation ecosystem — the veto was celebrated by major tech companies but criticized by AI safety researchers.

laws.title: Proposition 1 – Mental Health and Housing Bond
laws.subtitle: California passed a $6.38 billion bond to fund mental health housing
laws.fullDescription: California voters approved Proposition 1 in March 2024 (by a razor-thin margin of approximately 50.2%) — a $6.38 billion bond to fund housing for people with mental illness and substance use disorders. It also reformed the Mental Health Services Act (MHSA) to require counties to spend a larger share on housing rather than prevention. Critics — including mental health advocates — argued the measure would reduce funding for prevention and outpatient services while redirecting money to psychiatric facilities. Supporters argued it addressed California's homelessness crisis, which disproportionately involves people with untreated mental illness. The narrow victory reflected genuine division on mental health policy approaches.
laws.penalty: Misuse of Proposition 1 bond funds: audit and recovery by State Controller. Mental health facility licensing violations: DHCS fines and license revocation.
exceptions: Counties retain some discretion in implementation of mental health services mix
Existing MHSA-funded programs in pipeline may continue under transition provisions

quiz.q: What made California's Proposition 1 (March 2024) controversial among mental health advocates?
options: It mandated forced treatment for homeless individuals
It reformed the Mental Health Services Act to prioritize housing over prevention and outpatient services
It cut total mental health spending by 15%
It privatized all mental health services previously run by counties
quiz.explanation: Mental health advocates opposed Prop 1 because it redirected MHSA funds from prevention and outpatient services toward housing — arguing this would reduce access to early intervention and community-based services that prevent hospitalization.

laws.title: California's Advanced Clean Cars II Regulations
laws.subtitle: Ban on new gasoline-only car sales by 2035
laws.fullDescription: California's Advanced Clean Cars II (ACC II) regulation, adopted in 2022 by the California Air Resources Board (CARB), requires that 100% of new passenger cars and light trucks sold in California be zero-emission vehicles (ZEVs) by 2035. The regulation ramps up gradually: 35% ZEV by 2026, 68% by 2030, and 100% by 2035. Plug-in hybrids can count toward targets with limitations. Because California received a federal waiver allowing stricter-than-federal standards, other states can adopt California's standards. Over a dozen states have adopted or are considering adopting ACC II.
laws.penalty: Automakers selling non-compliant fleets face CARB fines per violation. Dealers selling non-compliant new vehicles: civil penalties up to $1,000 per vehicle per day. Automakers must submit annual compliance reports or face penalties
exceptions: Used vehicles are not covered — only new vehicle sales
Emergency vehicles have extended compliance timelines
Vehicles designed for off-road use have separate standards
laws.sourceLabel: California Air Resources Board - ACC II

quiz.q: By what year must 100% of new passenger cars sold in California be zero-emission under ACC II?
quiz.explanation: California's Advanced Clean Cars II regulation requires 100% of new passenger car and light truck sales to be zero-emission vehicles by 2035, with graduated requirements starting at 35% ZEV by 2026.

laws.title: California's Housing Element Law and Builder's Remedy
laws.subtitle: Cities that fail housing plans face override of local zoning
laws.fullDescription: California's Housing Element Law requires every city and county to plan for state-assigned housing units (Regional Housing Needs Allocation). Cities that fail to get their Housing Element certified by the Department of Housing and Community Development lose local zoning control through a provision called the 'Builder's Remedy' — which allows developers to bypass local zoning to build housing with affordability components. AB 2011 and SB 9 allow more housing by-right in single-family zones. California has sued cities (including Huntington Beach and Santa Monica) for failing to comply with state housing law.
laws.penalty: Non-compliant cities face loss of zoning control (Builder's Remedy), state lawsuits, and loss of certain state funding. Developers who violate approved housing element plans: permit revocation. Discrimination in housing approvals: fair housing enforcement plus civil liability
exceptions: Coastal Commission has separate oversight for coastal development permits
Historic preservation zones may have lighter housing density requirements
Tribal lands are exempt from state housing element law
laws.sourceLabel: California Department of Housing and Community Development

quiz.q: What is the 'Builder's Remedy' in California housing law?
options: A tax credit for affordable housing builders
A provision allowing developers to bypass local zoning in non-compliant cities
A state fund that pays for housing construction
A requirement for cities to build housing themselves
quiz.explanation: California's 'Builder's Remedy' allows housing developers to bypass local zoning restrictions in cities that have failed to get a state-certified Housing Element — effectively taking away local control over development as a penalty for non-compliance with state housing mandates.

laws.title: Coastal Development and CEQA Review
laws.subtitle: California's Coastal Act requires environmental review for all coastal development
laws.fullDescription: California's Coastal Act of 1976 and the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) together mandate environmental impact review for any development within the Coastal Zone. The California Coastal Commission must approve projects affecting the coast, including construction, grading, and beach access changes. Unpermitted development can result in cease-and-desist orders and mandatory restoration at the violator's expense. The Act also guarantees public access to the coastline and prevents private parties from blocking beach access.
laws.penalty: Unpermitted coastal development: fines up to $11,000 per day per violation; mandatory restoration costs
exceptions: Emergency repairs to existing structures
Certain agricultural activities with coastal permits

quiz.q: What agency enforces California's Coastal Act?
quiz.explanation: The California Coastal Commission is the state agency responsible for implementing and enforcing California's Coastal Act of 1976.

laws.title: AB 5 Gig Worker Reclassification Law
laws.subtitle: California requires gig companies to classify workers as employees
laws.fullDescription: California's Assembly Bill 5 (AB 5), enacted in 2019, established the 'ABC test' for worker classification, making it much harder for companies to classify workers as independent contractors. Under the ABC test, workers are presumed employees unless the company proves they work independently, perform work outside the company's core business, and are engaged in an independently established trade. App-based transportation and delivery companies fought back with Proposition 22, which voters passed in 2020 — but courts later struck down parts of Prop 22 as unconstitutional. The classification battle continues with significant implications for healthcare, retirement benefits, and workers' compensation.
laws.penalty: Misclassifying employees as independent contractors: back taxes, benefits, and fines; penalties can be hundreds of thousands per worker
exceptions: Prop 22 created a special category for app-based gig drivers (subject to ongoing litigation)
Professional services exemptions for doctors, lawyers, architects in their own businesses

quiz.q: What is the 'ABC test' under California's AB 5?
options: A test to determine if workers are independent contractors or employees
quiz.explanation: California's AB 5 established the 'ABC test' — a three-part test presuming workers are employees unless companies prove they work independently, outside the company's core business, and in an independently established trade.

laws.title: Advanced Clean Cars II and EV Mandate
laws.subtitle: California requires all new passenger vehicles to be zero-emission by 2035
laws.fullDescription: California's Air Resources Board (CARB) adopted the Advanced Clean Cars II (ACC II) regulation requiring 100% of new passenger car and light truck sales to be zero-emission vehicles (ZEVs) by 2035. Automakers must meet escalating ZEV percentage targets starting in 2026. The regulation also tightens tailpipe emission standards for non-ZEV vehicles still sold before 2035. Seventeen other US states have adopted or are adopting California's standards. The regulation is the most ambitious vehicle electrification mandate in the US and creates major compliance obligations for automakers selling in California.
laws.penalty: Automakers failing to meet ZEV sales percentage: fines per vehicle shortfall; penalties can total millions per model year
exceptions: Emergency vehicles and specialized equipment have different compliance timelines
Small volume manufacturers have modified compliance pathways

quiz.q: By what year does California require 100% of new passenger vehicle sales to be zero-emission?
quiz.explanation: California's Advanced Clean Cars II regulation requires 100% of new passenger car and light truck sales to be zero-emission vehicles (ZEVs) by 2035, with escalating percentage requirements starting in 2026.

laws.title: AI Transparency in Government
laws.subtitle: California requires disclosure when AI makes consequential decisions
laws.fullDescription: California's Automated Decision Systems law requires state agencies to notify individuals when automated decision tools are used in decisions affecting benefits, housing, employment, or similar matters. Agencies must explain the role AI played and provide an opportunity to appeal. The law also mandates impact assessments for high-risk AI systems deployed by the state.
laws.penalty: Administrative remedies; right to human review and appeal of AI-made decisions
exceptions: Purely informational AI tools
National security systems
Fraud detection in background roles

quiz.q: Under California's AI transparency rules, what must state agencies do when using automated decision systems?
options: Notify affected individuals and allow appeal
Only notify if the AI makes an error
Require a fee for human review
quiz.explanation: California law requires agencies to disclose AI use in consequential decisions and provide a right to human review and appeal.

laws.title: California Zero-Emission Vehicle Mandate
laws.subtitle: California requires all new car sales to be zero-emission by 2035
laws.fullDescription: California's Advanced Clean Cars II regulation mandates that 100% of new passenger cars and light trucks sold in California must be zero-emission vehicles by 2035. This is the most aggressive vehicle electrification mandate in the United States. California has unique authority under the Clean Air Act to set its own vehicle emission standards, and many other states follow California's rules. The regulation phases in requirements, with increasing ZEV percentages each year leading to the 2035 deadline.
laws.penalty: Automakers and dealers that sell non-compliant vehicles face fines; CARB can revoke sales authorization
exceptions: Used vehicle sales are not covered
Commercial trucks follow separate CARB regulations
Emergency vehicles have extended transition periods

quiz.q: By what year does California require 100% of new car sales to be zero-emission?
quiz.explanation: California's Advanced Clean Cars II regulation requires 100% of new passenger vehicle sales to be zero-emission by 2035.

laws.title: California Ghost Gun Regulations
laws.subtitle: California bans untraceable privately made firearms
laws.fullDescription: California enacted AB 1621 and related laws to address ghost guns — privately made firearms without serial numbers that are difficult to trace. The laws require serialization of home-manufactured firearms, ban unserialized firearm components, and restrict sales of ghost gun kits. California has been at the forefront of ghost gun regulation in the US, while Second Amendment advocates have challenged these laws in federal courts with mixed results.
laws.penalty: Possession of unserialized firearm: up to 1 year in jail; selling ghost gun kits: up to 3 years; manufacturing without serialization: fines and confiscation
exceptions: Firearms manufactured before serialization requirement took effect with grandfather provisions
Licensed FFL dealers
Law enforcement agencies

quiz.q: What is a ghost gun?
options: A gun used in unsolved crimes
A privately made firearm without a serial number that is difficult to trace
A digital gun in a video game
quiz.explanation: A ghost gun is a privately manufactured firearm without a serial number, making it difficult to trace in criminal investigations. California has enacted strict laws to require serialization and ban their sale.

laws.title: California Warehouse Worker Protection Act
laws.subtitle: California regulates warehouse quotas to protect worker safety
laws.fullDescription: California enacted the Warehouse Quotas Act (AB 701, 2021) requiring large warehouse employers to disclose work quotas to employees and prohibiting quotas that prevent workers from taking bathroom breaks, following safety laws, or resting during meal periods. The law was specifically aimed at Amazon and similar large warehouse operations. Workers can request a written description of their quota and challenge unlawful quotas. The law made California the first state to directly regulate warehouse quotas.
laws.penalty: Employers with unlawful quotas: civil penalties up to $100 per employee per violation; retaliation against workers who challenge quotas: additional penalties
exceptions: Warehouses with fewer than 100 employees at a single location
Quotas that do not prevent legally required breaks
Managerial flexibility during documented surge periods

quiz.q: What specific worker right did California's Warehouse Quotas Act explicitly protect?
options: Right to take bathroom breaks and rest periods without penalty from quotas
quiz.explanation: California's Warehouse Quotas Act prohibits work quotas that prevent employees from taking legally required bathroom breaks, rest periods, and meal breaks — directly targeting practices documented at large fulfillment warehouses.

laws.title: AB 1482 Rent Control Statewide
laws.subtitle: California's statewide just cause eviction and rent cap law
laws.fullDescription: California's AB 1482 (Tenant Protection Act) established statewide rent control for eligible properties, capping annual rent increases at 5% plus local CPI, up to a maximum of 10%. The law also requires landlords to have just cause to evict tenants who have lived in a unit for 12 months or more. Just cause includes non-payment of rent, lease violations, and owner move-in, but removes the ability to evict without reason. Properties built within the last 15 years, single-family homes owned by individuals, and condos are exempt.
laws.penalty: Landlords who violate rent caps or evict without just cause face civil liability to tenants including actual damages, punitive damages, and attorneys fees; local rent boards can impose additional fines
exceptions: Single-family homes and condos not owned by corporations are exempt
Units built within the last 15 years are exempt
Owner-occupied duplexes are exempt
Properties already covered by stricter local rent control follow local rules

quiz.q: What is the maximum annual rent increase allowed under California's AB 1482?
options: Equal to the consumer price index
No limit but must have just cause
quiz.explanation: AB 1482 caps annual rent increases at 5% plus the local CPI inflation rate, with an absolute maximum of 10% per year, regardless of how high inflation might be.

laws.title: Reproductive Health Laws Post-Dobbs
laws.subtitle: California's expanded abortion access and shield laws
laws.fullDescription: Following the US Supreme Court's Dobbs decision overturning Roe v. Wade, California enacted a comprehensive package of reproductive health laws. California declared itself a reproductive freedom state, added abortion rights to the state constitution, expanded Medi-Cal coverage for abortion at no cost, prohibited enforcement of other states' anti-abortion laws against California providers and patients, and created shield laws protecting California providers who assist out-of-state patients. California also funded an abortion travel fund for patients from restrictive states and prohibited employers from cooperating with out-of-state abortion investigations.
laws.penalty: California law enforcement may not cooperate with out-of-state abortion warrants; employers who cooperate with out-of-state anti-abortion investigations face civil liability; threatening California providers for offering legal services carries criminal penalties
exceptions: Medical providers retain professional discretion regarding procedures outside their scope or beliefs
Federal law enforcement actions are exempt from state shield provisions
Emergency medical care requirements override any other considerations

quiz.q: What did California add to its state constitution following the US Supreme Court's Dobbs decision?
options: Abortion rights as a state constitutional right
quiz.explanation: California amended its state constitution to explicitly protect abortion rights, ensuring that abortion access in California cannot be eliminated by state legislation even if federal courts allow other states to ban it — making California's protections legally stronger than before Dobbs.

laws.title: Right to Repair Law (SB 244)
laws.subtitle: California requiring manufacturers to provide repair parts and tools
laws.fullDescription: California enacted SB 244, one of the nation's strongest Right to Repair laws, requiring manufacturers of electronics and appliances to make repair parts, tools, and documentation available to independent repair shops and consumers for products costing more than $50 and sold after July 2021. The law covers smartphones, laptops, tablets, and major appliances. It prohibits manufacturers from using software locks or other digital means to prevent independent repairs. California's law is expected to set a de facto national standard given the state's market size.
laws.penalty: Manufacturers who violate right to repair requirements face civil enforcement by the Attorney General; fines up to $1,000 per violation per day; consumers can seek injunctive relief
exceptions: Certain safety-critical vehicle components are exempt from independent repair requirements
Medical devices have separate FDA repair oversight
Products sold exclusively for commercial or industrial use have modified requirements

quiz.q: What is the minimum price threshold for products covered by California's Right to Repair law?
options: All consumer electronics regardless of price
quiz.explanation: California's SB 244 Right to Repair law applies to electronics and appliances costing more than $50, requiring manufacturers to make parts, tools, and documentation available for independent repairs — setting a threshold that captures smartphones and laptops but not the cheapest disposable devices.

laws.title: California Extended Producer Responsibility Packaging Law (SB 54)
laws.subtitle: Mandating plastic reduction and producer funding for recycling
laws.fullDescription: California's SB 54 (Plastic Pollution Prevention and Packaging Producer Responsibility Act, 2022) established the nation's most comprehensive extended producer responsibility law for packaging. By 2032, all plastic packaging sold in California must be recyclable or compostable, with a 25% reduction in single-use plastic and a 65% recycling rate. Producers pay into a Producer Responsibility Organization (PRO) fund to finance recycling infrastructure. The law covers all plastic packaging sold by companies doing business in California.
laws.penalty: Producers who fail to meet plastic reduction targets face civil penalties of $50,000 per day of violation. The PRO organization faces fines of up to $1 million for non-compliance with annual reporting requirements.
exceptions: Medical devices and pharmaceuticals packaging exempt from source reduction requirements
Small producers with annual plastic packaging under 1 ton qualify for simplified compliance pathway
Packaging from companies with under $1 million annual US revenue subject to modified phase-in timeline

quiz.q: By what year must all plastic packaging in California meet recyclability or compostability standards under SB 54?
quiz.explanation: California's SB 54 requires all single-use plastic packaging to be recyclable or compostable by 2032, with interim milestones including a 25% plastic reduction and 65% recycling rate. It is considered the most comprehensive producer responsibility law for packaging in the US.

laws.title: California AI Transparency in Government Act (AB 2013)
laws.subtitle: Requiring disclosure of AI use in public agency decisions
laws.fullDescription: California enacted AB 2013 (2024), requiring state agencies that use generative AI to create public-facing content or make consequential decisions to disclose this use. State agencies must label AI-generated text, images, and video; document the AI systems used; publish summaries of AI training data; and notify members of the public when AI made or significantly influenced a decision affecting them. The law was part of a package of 18 AI-related bills signed by Governor Newsom in 2024.
laws.penalty: State agencies that fail to disclose AI use in public content: administrative sanctions from the California Department of Technology. Officials who knowingly misrepresent AI use: potential civil liability under the Government Code.
exceptions: AI used solely for internal administrative purposes (spell-check, formatting) not subject to public disclosure requirements
Law enforcement AI surveillance tools subject to separate CCOPS disclosure requirements
AI systems used in classified state security operations exempt from public disclosure

quiz.q: How many AI-related bills did Governor Newsom sign as part of California's 2024 AI legislation package?
quiz.explanation: Governor Newsom signed a package of 18 AI-related bills in 2024, including AB 2013 on AI transparency in government, as California sought to establish comprehensive AI governance — though Newsom vetoed a separate AI safety bill (SB 1047) that would have required safety testing of large AI models.

laws.title: California AB 2011 and SB 6 - Housing on Commercial Land
laws.subtitle: Allowing residential development on office and retail sites
laws.fullDescription: California enacted AB 2011 (Affordable Housing and High Road Jobs Act) and SB 6 (Middle Class Housing Act of 2022), both effective July 2023, allowing residential development on commercially zoned land (office, retail) by-right — bypassing local zoning opposition. AB 2011 targets 100% affordable and market-rate projects near transit corridors; SB 6 applies more broadly. The laws created a ministerial approval process eliminating discretionary review for qualifying projects, responding to California's severe housing shortage.
laws.penalty: Local governments that improperly deny qualifying ministerial housing applications: mandamus action forcing approval and developer attorneys' fee recovery. Officials who create procedural barriers to delay qualifying projects: exposure to civil liability.
exceptions: Projects in high-fire hazard zones require additional safety review before ministerial approval
Sites with significant cultural or tribal resources subject to consultation requirements
Projects near airports subject to flight path compatibility review

quiz.q: What type of approval process do AB 2011 and SB 6 create for qualifying housing projects?
options: Ministerial approval bypassing local discretionary review
quiz.explanation: AB 2011 and SB 6 create a ministerial approval process for qualifying housing projects on commercial land — meaning local governments must approve projects that meet objective standards without discretionary review, preventing cities from blocking housing through subjective criteria or community opposition.

laws.title: AI Disclosure and Chatbot Transparency Act (AB 2602)
laws.subtitle: California requires AI-generated content disclosures
laws.fullDescription: California enacted AB 2602 requiring businesses using AI to generate content to disclose when content is AI-generated in specified contexts including political advertising, customer service chatbots, and AI voices in entertainment. Separately, SB 942 required AI developers to implement content provenance standards. The laws made California the first US state with comprehensive AI content disclosure mandates.
laws.penalty: Violations of AI disclosure requirements: civil penalties up to $5,000 per violation; political advertising violations: up to $50,000
exceptions: Academic and research uses of AI-generated content exempt
Internal corporate communications not subject to disclosure requirements

quiz.q: What contexts does California's AB 2602 require AI content disclosures for?
options: Political advertising, customer service chatbots, and AI voices in entertainment
quiz.explanation: California's AB 2602 requires AI disclosure specifically in contexts including political advertising, customer service chatbots, and AI-generated voices in entertainment — targeting the highest-risk disclosure gaps.

laws.title: Coastal Resilience Act and Sea Level Rise Adaptation
laws.subtitle: California funds managed retreat and coastal protection measures
laws.fullDescription: California enacted the Coastal Resilience Act, dedicating $2.5 billion over 10 years to managed retreat from high-risk coastal zones, wetland restoration as natural sea barriers, and hardening critical coastal infrastructure. Property owners in designated high-risk zones must disclose sea level rise risks in real estate sales. The law also reformed the Coastal Commission to accelerate resilience project permitting.
laws.penalty: Failure to disclose sea level rise risk in coastal property sales: real estate licence sanctions and civil liability
exceptions: Commercial fishing infrastructure receives extended operational period before managed retreat requirements
Public beaches and parks exempted from private managed retreat buyout requirements

quiz.q: What disclosure requirement does California's Coastal Resilience Act impose on property sellers?
options: Sea level rise risk must be disclosed in coastal property sales
Wildfire risk disclosure for coastal homes
quiz.explanation: California's Coastal Resilience Act requires property sellers in designated high-risk coastal zones to disclose sea level rise risks to buyers, ensuring potential purchasers understand the long-term climate threat to the property.

laws.title: Assault Weapon Ban Reinstatement (AB 1621)
laws.subtitle: California renews restrictions on semi-automatic weapons
laws.fullDescription: California enacted updated assault weapon restrictions after the federal ban's expiration, imposing state-level prohibitions on semi-automatic rifles with detachable magazines and specific features. The law was repeatedly challenged under the Bruen Supreme Court standard for Second Amendment cases, with courts issuing conflicting rulings. California continued defending the restrictions through the appeals process.
laws.penalty: Possession of prohibited assault weapon: felony, up to 3 years imprisonment; manufacture or transfer: up to 8 years
exceptions: Law enforcement and military exempt from civilian assault weapon restrictions
Grandfathered pre-ban weapons that were registered by a specified deadline exempt from new possession rules

quiz.q: Under what Supreme Court standard are California's assault weapon laws now challenged?
options: Bruen text, history, and tradition standard
quiz.explanation: New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen (2022) established the 'text, history, and tradition' standard for Second Amendment challenges, which has been used to challenge California's assault weapon restrictions in multiple court cases.

laws.title: California Ocean Protection and Offshore Wind Development Act
laws.subtitle: Floating offshore wind leasing and marine sanctuary expansion
laws.fullDescription: California enacted the Ocean Protection and Offshore Wind Development Act 2025, combining marine conservation with clean energy ambitions. The law expands California's network of Marine Protected Areas to cover 30% of state waters, establishes a leasing framework for floating offshore wind development in federal waters off the California coast (Morro Bay, Humboldt), creates a Just Transition Fund for commercial fishing communities displaced by offshore wind zones, mandates a Blue Carbon Accounting Program measuring sequestration in kelp forests and seagrass, and sets a 2,500 MW offshore wind installation target by 2030. Floating platforms are required given California's deep coastal waters.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized fishing in expanded MPAs: vessel seizure plus $500,000 fine; offshore wind construction without migratory bird impact study: $5 million; marine pollution from construction: triple remediation cost
exceptions: Tribal fishing rights in traditional areas preserved under treaty obligations
Research vessels from accredited institutions have modified MPA access
Emergency coast guard operations exempt from offshore wind zone exclusions

quiz.q: Why does California require floating platforms for offshore wind development rather than fixed-bottom turbines?
options: California has deep coastal waters unsuitable for fixed-bottom turbines
Visual impact requirements prohibit near-shore placement
quiz.explanation: California's coastal waters drop off steeply to depths too great for conventional fixed-bottom wind turbine foundations, making floating platform technology necessary for offshore wind development along the California coast.

laws.title: California Universal Healthcare Single Payer Study and Pilot Act
laws.subtitle: Moving toward state-run universal health coverage
laws.fullDescription: California enacted the Universal Healthcare Study and Pilot Program Act 2025, the most concrete step any US state has taken toward single-payer healthcare. The law creates the California Health Care Financing Authority with power to negotiate pharmaceutical prices, establishes three county-level pilot programs implementing single-payer coverage for all residents regardless of immigration status, mandates a comprehensive actuarial study of full statewide implementation costs, requires all health insurers operating in California to provide transparent claims data to enable comparison, and establishes a Healthcare Transition Fund with $5 billion to support workers displaced from insurance industry jobs. The Act followed decades of failed single-payer legislation.
laws.penalty: Health insurer data non-compliance: $10 million per year plus license review; Financing Authority obstruction: $5 million; pilot program fraud: 20 years imprisonment
exceptions: Federal Medicare and Medicaid programs continue operating in parallel with pilots
Military veterans' VA health benefits unaffected by pilot programs
Health sharing ministries have modified compliance framework

quiz.q: What key feature do California's Universal Healthcare pilot programs include that distinguishes them from most US health programs?
quiz.explanation: California's Universal Healthcare pilot programs cover all residents regardless of immigration status — a notable feature that extends coverage to undocumented immigrants, a significant departure from federal health programs that restrict coverage based on legal status.

laws.title: California Biotech Leadership and Genetic Privacy Protection Act
laws.subtitle: Regulating genetic data while leading biotech innovation
laws.fullDescription: California enacted the Biotechnology Leadership and Genetic Data Privacy Act 2025, balancing its status as the world's biotech capital (San Diego, San Francisco Bay Area) with growing concerns about genomic data exploitation. The law creates the California Genomic Data Authority regulating use of genetic information by insurance companies, employers, and data brokers, prohibits sale of personal genomic data without specific informed consent for each use case, establishes the California Biotech Corridor Programme connecting UCSF, Stanford, Caltech, and UC San Diego with streamlined regulatory pathways for clinical trials, provides $3 billion in life sciences infrastructure grants, and introduces criminal penalties for genetic discrimination in employment or housing.
laws.penalty: Genomic data sale without specific consent: $50 million per violation; genetic discrimination in employment: $500,000 per affected person; clinical trial data fraud: 20 years imprisonment
exceptions: Law enforcement use of genetic databases for violent crime investigation under warrant
Academic non-profit research with IRB approval has modified consent requirements
Medical necessity sharing between treating physicians
De-identified aggregate research data exempt from individual consent
laws.sourceLabel: California Governor's Office of Planning and Research

quiz.q: What two major California metropolitan areas anchor the biotech corridors connected by the 2025 Biotech Leadership Act?
options: San Diego and San Francisco Bay Area
quiz.explanation: San Diego (home to major biotech companies and the Scripps Research Institute) and the San Francisco Bay Area (home to Genentech, Gilead, and hundreds of biotech startups near UCSF and Stanford) anchor California's world-leading biotechnology ecosystem.

laws.title: 100% Clean Energy Grid Acceleration Act
laws.subtitle: Accelerating renewable energy storage and grid modernization
laws.fullDescription: California enacted legislation to accelerate its already-ambitious clean energy goals by requiring utilities to procure additional long-duration energy storage, expanding offshore wind development in federal waters off the California coast, and streamlining permits for transmission lines connecting renewable energy zones to population centers. The law also establishes community benefit agreements for renewable energy projects near disadvantaged communities.
laws.penalty: Utilities that miss storage procurement targets face fines of $1 million per day per gigawatt-hour of shortfall. Transmission project developers who violate community benefit agreements face permit revocation.
exceptions: Small community choice aggregators under 50,000 customers have extended timelines
Agricultural solar installations on farmland retain expedited permit processes

quiz.q: What type of energy storage does California's Clean Energy Grid Act emphasize for grid stability?
quiz.explanation: Long-duration energy storage (capable of storing energy for 10+ hours) is critical for California's grid because solar and wind power don't always match demand patterns — the law requires utilities to procure significant new long-duration storage capacity.

laws.title: AI Accountability and Algorithmic Discrimination Prevention Act
laws.subtitle: Regulating high-risk AI systems in employment and lending
laws.fullDescription: California enacted landmark AI accountability legislation requiring companies to conduct impact assessments before deploying high-risk AI systems in employment, lending, housing, and healthcare decisions. The law mandates transparency about when AI is used in consequential decisions, creates a right to human review of adverse AI decisions, requires bias audits for automated screening tools, and establishes enforcement through the Civil Rights Department.
laws.penalty: Companies that deploy high-risk AI without required impact assessments face fines up to $25,000 per violation. Discriminatory AI systems that cause demonstrable harm face class action liability without damage caps.
exceptions: Small businesses with under 100 employees have a two-year compliance grace period
AI used purely for internal employee productivity without consequential decisions is exempt

quiz.q: What right does California's AI Accountability Act give people who receive adverse decisions from AI systems?
options: Right to appeal to a federal court
Right to human review of adverse AI decisions
Right to know the AI's training data
Right to sue the AI developer directly
quiz.explanation: California's AI Accountability Act gives individuals the right to request human review of adverse decisions made by AI systems in high-stakes contexts like employment rejections, loan denials, or insurance decisions.

laws.title: Social Housing and Public Developer Authority Act
laws.subtitle: State-owned affordable housing development
laws.fullDescription: California enacted legislation creating a public housing developer — the California Housing Authority — empowered to build mixed-income social housing on public land without relying on private developers. Inspired by Vienna's social housing model, the law creates a revolving public finance mechanism, allows the state to acquire underutilized properties, establishes mixed-income requirements, and streamlines permitting for publicly-developed housing.
laws.penalty: Local governments that use discriminatory zoning to block state housing authority projects face loss of state housing funding. Contractors who engage in bid-rigging on public housing projects face debarment and criminal prosecution.
exceptions: Historic districts retain design review authority over public housing aesthetics
Small rural communities under 5,000 population are exempt from state housing mandate requirements

quiz.q: What European city is famous for its social housing model that California's act drew inspiration from?
quiz.explanation: Vienna, Austria is famous for its Gemeindebauten (municipal housing) system where about 60% of residents live in publicly owned or subsidized housing. Vienna's model is studied worldwide as an example of how public housing can create stable, mixed-income communities.

laws.title: California AI Transparency and Accountability Act
laws.subtitle: Algorithmic Decision Disclosure Law
laws.fullDescription: Requires companies using AI systems for consequential decisions — employment, housing, credit, healthcare — to disclose when AI is involved and provide human review options. The law mandates bias audits for high-risk AI systems, requires plain-language explanations of AI decisions, and establishes a state AI Oversight Office. California's law influences national and international AI governance standards.
laws.penalty: Fines up to $250,000 per violation for companies failing AI disclosure requirements; injunctive relief
exceptions: AI tools used purely for internal company operations without external decisions
Research and development AI systems not deployed publicly

quiz.q: What must California companies provide when AI makes consequential decisions?
quiz.explanation: California's AI Transparency Act requires disclosure when AI makes consequential decisions and provides human review options.

laws.title: California Sustainable Groundwater Management Enforcement Act
laws.subtitle: SGMA Implementation and Water Rights Law
laws.fullDescription: Strengthens enforcement of California's Sustainable Groundwater Management Act as overdraft basins face mandatory cutbacks. The law establishes penalties for groundwater pumping violations, creates the State Water Board's adjudication authority for critically overdrafted basins, funds fallowing programs in the San Joaquin Valley, and creates transition assistance for agricultural communities dependent on unsustainable groundwater.
laws.penalty: Fines up to $10,000 per day for pumping violations; well shutdown orders; criminal prosecution for fraudulent reporting
exceptions: Domestic and municipal wells under specified thresholds
Emergency pumping during declared drought with mitigation plans

quiz.q: What does SGMA stand for in California water law?
quiz.explanation: SGMA stands for Sustainable Groundwater Management Act, California's landmark 2014 law to manage overdrafted groundwater basins.

laws.title: California Fast Food Accountability and Standards Recovery Act
laws.subtitle: Fast Food Worker Minimum Wage and Council Law
laws.fullDescription: Establishes a $20 minimum wage for fast food workers and creates the Fast Food Council with industry and worker representation to set standards. The law applies to chains with 60+ locations nationally, creates sector-wide standards for wages, hours, and working conditions, establishes the council as a permanent body, and creates rulemaking authority without requiring individual franchise bargaining.
laws.penalty: Fines up to $10,000 per violation for franchises failing to pay minimum wage; Labor Commissioner enforcement
exceptions: Independent restaurants not part of national chains
Fast food establishments inside grocery stores or hotels

quiz.q: What minimum wage did California's FAST Recovery Act establish for fast food workers?
quiz.explanation: California's FAST Recovery Act established a $20 per hour minimum wage for fast food workers at large national chains.

laws.title: California Proposition 36 Drug Crimes and Homelessness Act
laws.subtitle: Felony Drug Treatment and Retail Theft Law
laws.fullDescription: Voter-approved measure restoring felony penalties for certain drug possession and retail theft, modifying the 2014 Prop 47 reforms. The law creates new felony fentanyl possession charges, makes third retail theft a felony, requires treatment instead of incarceration for drug offenders, creates the Treatment-Mandated Felony designation, and establishes accountability for drug dealers causing overdose deaths.
laws.penalty: Felony charges for fentanyl possession and third retail theft; felony homicide for drug dealers causing overdose deaths
exceptions: First and second retail theft remain misdemeanors
Treatment completion converts felony to misdemeanor for eligible offenders

quiz.q: What does California's Proposition 36 restore for certain drug possessions?
quiz.explanation: California Proposition 36 restores felony penalties for certain drug possessions like fentanyl, modifying the 2014 Prop 47 that had reduced many drug crimes to misdemeanors.

laws.title: AI Transparency and Accountability Act
laws.subtitle: California Requires Disclosure of AI-Generated Content
laws.fullDescription: California enacted comprehensive artificial intelligence transparency legislation requiring disclosure when AI generates or substantially alters content in political advertising, news media, and commercial contexts. The law mandates watermarking of AI-generated images and video, and creates liability for deepfakes used in elections or to defame individuals.
laws.penalty: Civil penalties up to $250,000 for political deepfakes; injunctive relief available
exceptions: Satire and parody with clear labeling
Academic and research uses

quiz.q: What does California's AI Transparency Act require for political advertising?
options: Disclosure and watermarking of AI-generated content
quiz.explanation: California's AI transparency law requires disclosure and watermarking when AI generates or substantially alters content in political advertising and other contexts.

laws.title: Advanced Clean Cars II and 2035 ICE Ban
laws.subtitle: California Bans New Gas-Powered Car Sales
laws.fullDescription: California's Advanced Clean Cars II regulation mandates that all new passenger vehicles sold in the state be zero-emission by 2035. The rule was approved by CARB and adopted by over a dozen other states. The Trump administration sought to revoke California's federal waiver to set stricter standards, leading to legal battles.
laws.penalty: Automakers face fines for non-compliance with annual ZEV sales mandates
exceptions: Used car market not affected
Emergency vehicles phased in later
Federal waiver legal challenge ongoing

quiz.q: What does California's Advanced Clean Cars II mandate?
options: All vehicles must be electric now
No new gas-powered car sales after 2035
quiz.explanation: California's ACCII regulation bans new gasoline-powered passenger vehicle sales after 2035, requiring all new cars to be zero-emission.

laws.title: Mental Health Services Act Reform
laws.subtitle: California Overhauls Mental Health Funding
laws.fullDescription: California voters approved Proposition 1 in March 2024, reforming the Mental Health Services Act and authorizing $6.4 billion in bonds to build treatment facilities. The reform shifted priorities toward housing and treatment for the most severely mentally ill rather than early intervention. Critics debated whether forced treatment provisions were appropriate.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties; treatment compliance requirements for some recipients
exceptions: Voluntary treatment preference maintained
HIPAA privacy protections

quiz.q: What did California's Proposition 1 authorize for mental health?
options: Mandatory psychiatric holds for all homeless
$6.4 billion in bonds for treatment facilities
Insurance mandate for mental health coverage
quiz.explanation: California's Proposition 1 reformed the Mental Health Services Act and authorized $6.4 billion in bonds to build mental health and addiction treatment facilities.

laws.title: Fast Food Minimum Wage Law AB 1228
laws.subtitle: California Raises Fast Food Worker Minimum Wage to $20
laws.fullDescription: California raised the minimum wage for fast food workers to $20 per hour under AB 1228, creating a sector-specific minimum above the statewide $16 minimum. The law established a Fast Food Council to recommend future increases. Major chains including McDonald's and Chipotle raised prices and reduced hours in response.
laws.penalty: Labor Commissioner enforcement; civil penalties for violations
exceptions: Bakeries that sell bread excluded
Franchise owners lobbied for exemptions

quiz.q: What minimum wage did California establish specifically for fast food workers?
quiz.explanation: California raised the minimum wage specifically for fast food workers to $20 per hour under AB 1228, above the general statewide minimum wage.

laws.title: ADU Boom and Missing Middle Housing
laws.subtitle: California Legalizes Backyard Homes Statewide
laws.fullDescription: California's series of ADU (Accessory Dwelling Unit) laws legalized backyard homes, garage conversions, and split lots statewide, overriding local zoning restrictions. The ADU boom added hundreds of thousands of new units. The state also legalized fourplexes statewide as part of missing middle housing reform.
laws.penalty: Cities fined for rejecting conforming ADU applications
exceptions: HOA restrictions challenged
Coastal zone permits still required

quiz.q: What type of housing did California massively expand to address the housing crisis?
options: ADUs (Accessory Dwelling Units) like backyard homes
quiz.explanation: California's ADU laws legalized backyard homes, garage conversions, and split lots statewide, overriding local zoning to boost housing supply.

laws.title: Hollywood Strikes and AI Threat to Creative Work
laws.subtitle: SAG-AFTRA and WGA secure AI protections in landmark contracts
