laws.fullDescription: The 2023 Hollywood strikes by SAG-AFTRA and the Writers Guild of America (WGA) were significantly driven by AI concerns — studios wanting to scan actor likenesses for perpetual use and replace writers with AI tools. The strikes lasted months before studios agreed to protections: writers cannot be replaced by AI, and actors must consent to and be compensated for digital likeness use. The contracts became models for AI protections in other creative industries.
laws.penalty: Studios using AI-generated likenesses without consent face contract violations and SAG-AFTRA enforcement
exceptions: Background crowds can be digitally enhanced without individual consents
Historical documentary use of archival footage exempt from new AI likeness rules

laws.title: AI Regulation and SB 1047 Battle
laws.subtitle: California's AI safety bill debate shapes national policy
laws.fullDescription: California's SB 1047 would have required safety evaluations for large AI models, but Governor Newsom vetoed it under pressure from the tech industry, which argued it would harm California's AI leadership. The debate ignited nationally about whether states or the federal government should regulate AI. California subsequently passed narrower AI transparency bills. The state hosts most major AI labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta AI) and its regulatory choices ripple across the global AI industry.
laws.penalty: AI companies that misrepresent safety capabilities face consumer protection law liability
exceptions: Research models not deployed publicly have lighter requirements
Open-source models have different regulatory treatment than proprietary commercial AI

laws.title: Atmospheric River Management and Flood Infrastructure
laws.subtitle: California tries to capture storms after years of drought
laws.fullDescription: California whipsaws between drought and flood due to climate change. Atmospheric rivers — long streams of concentrated water vapor — deliver 50% of California's precipitation in just a few storms. The 2022-23 atmospheric river sequence ended a three-year drought but caused massive flooding. California is investing in flood-MAR (managed aquifer recharge) to capture storm water underground. New reservoirs and groundwater banking aim to store water from wet years for dry years. This water storage infrastructure costs billions.
laws.penalty: Groundwater extraction in overdrafted basins must follow sustainable groundwater management plans
exceptions: Emergency groundwater use during drought conditions has relaxed enforcement
Agricultural water users with senior riparian rights maintain priority access during shortages

laws.title: Plastic Pollution Legislation and Extended Producer Responsibility
laws.subtitle: California leading US on plastics regulation and waste reduction
laws.fullDescription: California has passed some of the nation's most ambitious plastic pollution legislation, including SB 54 (2022) which requires 30% of plastic packaging to be recyclable or compostable by 2028 and 65% by 2032, rising to 100% by 2032. California also imposes extended producer responsibility (EPR) requirements, making manufacturers financially responsible for end-of-life management of their packaging. The state has banned single-use plastic bags, Styrofoam food containers, and various other single-use plastics. California's regulations often become national standards due to its market size — companies frequently adopt California standards nationwide rather than producing separate products for the California market. Enforcement includes significant fines for violations. Critics argue the requirements impose costs on businesses and consumers, while supporters say external costs of plastic pollution justify regulation.
laws.penalty: Violations of plastic packaging requirements can carry fines up to $50,000 per day
exceptions: Some medical and safety applications are exempt from packaging restrictions

quiz.q: What does California's SB 54 require for plastic packaging by 2032?
quiz.explanation: California's SB 54 requires 100% of plastic packaging to be recyclable or compostable by 2032, with interim targets of 30% by 2028 and 65% by 2032, making it one of the nation's most ambitious plastics laws.

laws.title: AI Regulation Leadership and SB 1047 Controversy
laws.subtitle: California battling over who regulates frontier AI systems
laws.fullDescription: California attempted to pass SB 1047, landmark legislation that would have required safety evaluations and shutdown capabilities for the most powerful AI models, imposing liability on developers if their AI caused serious harm. The bill passed the legislature with broad support but Governor Gavin Newsom vetoed it in September 2024, arguing it would stifle AI innovation and that federal regulation was more appropriate. The veto disappointed AI safety advocates and highlighted the tension between California's twin roles as the home of the world's most powerful AI companies and a progressive regulatory leader. California houses virtually all major AI labs — OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta AI — making its regulatory decisions globally significant. Despite the SB 1047 veto, California has passed other AI laws covering deepfakes, algorithmic discrimination, and transparency requirements.
laws.penalty: Existing California laws on deepfakes, employment discrimination, and consumer privacy apply to AI; future AI-specific laws may add requirements
exceptions: National security applications and some research activities have different regulatory treatment

quiz.q: What happened to California's SB 1047 AI safety bill?
options: It was signed into law as the strictest AI regulation globally
Governor Newsom vetoed it after it passed the legislature
It was struck down by federal courts as preempted
It is still pending in committee
quiz.explanation: Governor Newsom vetoed SB 1047 in September 2024, arguing it would harm AI innovation and that federal regulation was more appropriate, despite the bill having passed the legislature with broad support.

laws.title: Wildfire Risk Insurance Crisis and Home Hardening Mandate
laws.subtitle: California's insurance market collapsing from wildfire exposure
laws.fullDescription: California's home insurance market is in crisis as major insurers including State Farm, Allstate, and Farmers have stopped writing new policies or withdrawn from the state entirely. The combination of increasing wildfire risk from climate change, escalating rebuilding costs, and California's regulatory limits on premium increases have made the California market unprofitable. The state-run FAIR Plan (insurer of last resort) has seen enrollment surge but faces solvency concerns after catastrophic fire seasons. The January 2025 Los Angeles wildfires — which burned in Pacific Palisades, Altadena, and other communities destroying thousands of homes — were the most destructive in California history, accelerating the insurance crisis. California has passed legislation requiring homes to be hardened against wildfire (ember-resistant vents, fire-resistant roofing) and allowing insurers more flexibility in rate-setting to attract them back.
laws.penalty: Building codes carry permit requirements; insurance fraud carries criminal penalties; unlicensed insurance activities carry regulatory action
exceptions: Historical buildings may receive modified hardening requirements to preserve architectural character

quiz.q: What event in January 2025 became the most destructive wildfire in California history?
options: The Los Angeles wildfires in Pacific Palisades and Altadena
The Dixie Fire in Plumas County
quiz.explanation: The January 2025 Los Angeles wildfires, burning in Pacific Palisades, Altadena, and other communities and destroying thousands of homes, became the most destructive wildfires in California history, accelerating the insurance market crisis.

laws.title: Groundwater Sustainability Act Implementation
laws.subtitle: California mandates sustainable groundwater management by 2040
laws.fullDescription: California's Sustainable Groundwater Management Act (SGMA) requires local agencies to bring groundwater basins into balance by 2040. Decades of over-pumping have caused land subsidence in the Central Valley—sinking as much as a foot per year—and dried up domestic wells. Groundwater sustainability agencies must submit and implement plans to reduce pumping. Agricultural interests face limits that may take tens of thousands of acres of farmland out of production.
laws.penalty: Non-compliant basins face state intervention with mandatory management plans; water rights curtailments enforced
exceptions: Small domestic well users receive some protections during transition
Critical water shortage provisions allow emergency pumping with mitigation plans

quiz.q: What physical consequence of groundwater over-pumping has affected California's Central Valley?
options: Land subsidence sinking at up to a foot per year
quiz.explanation: Decades of groundwater over-pumping in California's Central Valley has caused land subsidence—the ground sinking—at rates as high as a foot per year in some areas, damaging infrastructure and threatening the region's agricultural future.

laws.title: AI Regulation SB 1047 and Generative AI Laws
laws.subtitle: California becomes global AI governance battleground
laws.fullDescription: California has been at the center of AI regulation debates. SB 1047, a major AI safety bill requiring developers of large AI models to conduct safety testing and implement safeguards, passed the legislature but was vetoed by Governor Newsom in 2024. Newsom argued it could harm California's AI industry. However numerous other AI-related bills on bias, deepfakes, transparency and autonomous vehicles have passed. California's decisions effectively set US AI policy given Silicon Valley's dominance in AI development.
laws.penalty: Deepfake laws carry civil liability; automated decision-making in employment subject to notice requirements
exceptions: Research and development of AI models not covered by most operational requirements
Narrowly tailored applications may qualify for regulatory sandbox programs

quiz.q: What happened to California's major AI safety bill SB 1047 that required safety testing for large AI models?
options: It was vetoed by Governor Newsom
It was struck down by courts
quiz.explanation: SB 1047 passed the California legislature but was vetoed by Governor Newsom in 2024, who argued it could harm California's AI industry despite strong support from AI safety advocates.

laws.title: Prop 33 and Rent Control Battles
laws.subtitle: California voters repeatedly reject expanded rent control
laws.fullDescription: California voters have rejected rent control expansion initiatives multiple times, including Proposition 33 in November 2024, which would have removed restrictions on local rent control laws. Despite California's severe housing affordability crisis, voters have consistently chosen property rights over expanded tenant protections. Landlord interests spent tens of millions defeating each measure. Meanwhile California's housing crisis has driven record homelessness and outmigration of middle-class residents to other states.
laws.penalty: Existing state Costa-Hawkins law limits local rent control to buildings built before 1995; exempts single-family homes
exceptions: Existing local rent control ordinances in cities like San Francisco and Los Angeles remain valid
Emergency rental protections can be enacted during declared emergencies

quiz.q: What California law prevents localities from expanding rent control to newer buildings?
quiz.explanation: The Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act restricts local rent control to buildings built before 1995 and exempts single-family homes—limiting how extensively cities like LA and San Francisco can control rents even as the housing crisis has worsened.

laws.title: Climate Corporate Accountability Act
laws.subtitle: Companies Must Disclose Emissions
laws.fullDescription: California's SB 253 requires large companies doing business in the state to publicly disclose their greenhouse gas emissions across all three scopes — direct emissions, indirect energy emissions, and full value chain emissions. Companies with over $1 billion in revenue must report Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 2026 and Scope 3 by 2027, making California the first US state to mandate comprehensive corporate climate disclosure.
laws.penalty: Fines up to $500,000 per year for non-compliance or inaccurate reporting
exceptions: Companies below $1 billion revenue threshold
Non-profit organizations
Government entities

laws.title: SB 1386 Mental Health Services Act Expansion
laws.subtitle: Tax the Rich, Fund Mental Health
laws.fullDescription: California's Mental Health Services Act (Prop 63, 2004), funded by a 1% tax on incomes over $1 million, generates over $2 billion annually for county mental health services. SB 1386 and subsequent legislation expanded mobile crisis response teams and mental health courts. California also passed CARE Court (Community Assistance, Recovery, and Empowerment) in 2022, allowing courts to order mental health treatment plans for severely mentally ill individuals living on the streets. With the nation's largest homeless population, California has been pioneering new mental health intervention approaches.
laws.penalty: Mental health diversion program; CARE Court orders enforceable; involuntary holds under 5150
exceptions: Voluntary treatment preferred; CARE Court only for severe cases
Religious institutions exempt from compliance mandates

laws.title: California Gig Worker Rights — AB 5 and Prop 22
laws.subtitle: The Battle Over Independent Contractor Status
laws.fullDescription: California's AB 5 (2019) applied the 'ABC test' to classify workers as employees vs. independent contractors, making it harder for gig companies like Uber, Lyft, and DoorDash to classify drivers as contractors. Gig companies spent $200 million on Proposition 22 (2020), which exempted app-based drivers from AB 5. Prop 22 was later struck down by a lower court (2021) but upheld by the California Supreme Court (2024). The legal battle redefined the national debate on gig worker protections, with California remaining the battleground. AB 5 covered other industries including trucking.
laws.penalty: Employers misclassifying employees as contractors face back taxes, benefits liability, and penalties
exceptions: Prop 22 exempts app-based transportation and delivery drivers
Numerous industry exemptions were added to AB 5 after passage

laws.title: California Master Plan for Higher Education
laws.subtitle: Free University Access as a State Goal
laws.fullDescription: California's 1960 Master Plan for Higher Education created a three-tier system — University of California (research), California State University (teaching), and Community Colleges — with the principle that any qualified California student should have access to higher education at low or no cost. The plan created the world's largest higher education system. While community colleges remain inexpensive ($46/unit), UC and CSU costs have risen dramatically since the 1990s due to state funding cuts. California has ongoing debates about affirmative action in university admissions (Proposition 16 failed in 2020).
laws.penalty: Private universities must comply with state licensing; financial aid fraud prosecuted; discriminatory admissions: civil rights lawsuits
exceptions: Private universities under separate accreditation framework
International student tuition higher than resident rates

laws.title: California Values Act (SB 54)
laws.subtitle: California's sanctuary state protections
laws.fullDescription: California's SB 54 (2017), signed by Governor Jerry Brown, prohibits state and local law enforcement from using resources to investigate, detain, or arrest people for immigration enforcement purposes, or from sharing information with ICE without a warrant. California became the first state to formally enact sanctuary state protections. The law does allow cooperation for individuals with certain serious criminal convictions. The Trump administration sued California, but the 9th Circuit upheld the law. Approximately 3 million undocumented immigrants live in California.
laws.penalty: State agencies and law enforcement that violate SB 54 by cooperating with federal immigration enforcement beyond permitted scope face legal liability; local governments may not enter contracts with ICE for immigration detention
exceptions: Law enforcement may share information about individuals convicted of serious/violent felonies
Federal agents may still conduct immigration enforcement in California—the law restricts state assistance only

quiz.q: California's SB 54 primarily restricts what?
options: State law enforcement from assisting ICE with immigration enforcement
quiz.explanation: SB 54 restricts California state and local law enforcement from using resources to assist ICE with civil immigration enforcement, effectively making California a 'sanctuary state' — though federal agents can still operate independently in California.

laws.title: Proposition 64: Adult Use of Marijuana Act
laws.subtitle: California's cannabis legalization framework
laws.fullDescription: California's Proposition 64 (2016) legalized recreational cannabis for adults 21+, creating a licensed retail market with a 15% excise tax plus state sales tax. California has the world's largest legal cannabis market but struggles with an illegal market (estimated 3x larger than legal) due to high taxes, licensing delays, and local bans (many cities prohibit cannabis retail). Cannabis remains Schedule I federally, creating banking, interstate commerce, and federal employment complications. Proposition 47 (2014) also reduced drug possession to misdemeanors.
laws.penalty: Unlicensed cannabis sales: felony, up to 3 years; possession over legal limits: misdemeanor; DUI while impaired by cannabis: same penalties as alcohol DUI; minors possessing cannabis: infraction
exceptions: Adults 21+ may possess up to 28.5g flower and 8g concentrate
Adults may grow up to 6 plants at home for personal use
Medical cannabis patients have higher possession limits

quiz.q: Despite California having the world's largest legal cannabis market, the illegal market is estimated to be how much larger?
quiz.explanation: California's illegal cannabis market is estimated to be approximately 3 times larger than the legal market, driven by the legal market's high taxes (15% excise + sales tax), expensive licensing processes, and bans on legal retail in many cities and counties.

laws.title: California LGBTQ+ Protections
laws.subtitle: California's comprehensive LGBTQ+ rights framework
laws.fullDescription: California leads the US in LGBTQ+ legal protections. California was the first state to add sexual orientation to hate crime laws (1984), prohibit employment discrimination based on sexual orientation (1992), and provide comprehensive domestic partner rights (2001). The California Supreme Court legalized same-sex marriage in 2008 (In re Marriage Cases), overturned by Prop 8, then restored by federal courts. California law prohibits conversion therapy for minors, bans LGBT panic defense, requires gender-neutral bathrooms in schools, and protects transgender students' rights to use facilities matching their gender identity.
laws.penalty: Employment discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity: civil liability up to $150,000 per violation; hate crimes against LGBTQ+ individuals: enhanced felony penalties; conversion therapy on minors by licensed therapists: license revocation
exceptions: Religious organizations have some exemptions from non-discrimination requirements in employment of their own members
Small employers (fewer than 5 employees) have limited exemptions from some provisions

quiz.q: California prohibited employment discrimination based on sexual orientation in which year?
quiz.explanation: California prohibited employment discrimination based on sexual orientation in 1992, making it one of the earliest states to do so. This predated federal protections by decades — the Supreme Court only ruled that federal civil rights law covers sexual orientation in Bostock v. Clayton County (2020).

laws.title: Shield Law and Reporter Privilege
laws.subtitle: California's Shield Law gives journalists broad protection from revealing sources
laws.fullDescription: California has one of the strongest journalist shield laws in the United States. The California Shield Law (Evidence Code Section 1070) provides absolute protection for reporters' sources and unpublished information from compelled disclosure in court proceedings. The California constitution also contains an explicit provision protecting journalists. California journalists cannot be held in contempt for refusing to reveal confidential sources. The state also has strong public records laws under the California Public Records Act. Press freedom is robust, with Los Angeles and San Francisco as major media hubs.
laws.penalty: Journalists cannot be compelled to reveal sources; violation of the Shield Law would constitute contempt reversal
exceptions: Federal courts and grand jury proceedings may not recognize state shield protections

quiz.q: What does California's Shield Law protect journalists from?
options: Being compelled to reveal confidential sources
quiz.explanation: California's Shield Law (Evidence Code Section 1070) gives journalists absolute protection from being compelled to reveal confidential sources or unpublished information in court proceedings — one of the strongest press protections in the US.

laws.title: CCPA and Social Media Privacy Rights
laws.subtitle: California leads the US in social media and internet user privacy protections
laws.fullDescription: California's Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA, 2018) and its successor the California Privacy Rights Act (CPRA, 2020) give Californians the right to know what personal data companies collect, the right to delete it, and the right to opt out of its sale. California's Age-Appropriate Design Code Act (AB 2273, 2022) requires child privacy protections from social media platforms — a law that has been challenged in courts. California also has laws requiring social media platforms to disclose their content moderation policies. The California AI Transparency Act requires disclosure of AI-generated content.
laws.penalty: CPRA fines up to $7,500 per intentional violation; AADC violations subject to civil penalties
exceptions: First Amendment challenges have limited some provisions

quiz.q: What rights does California's CPRA give consumers regarding social media data?
options: Only the right to see their data
Right to know, delete, and opt out of sale of personal data
quiz.explanation: California's Consumer Privacy Rights Act (CPRA) gives consumers the right to know what personal data companies collect about them, the right to delete it, and the right to opt out of the sale of their personal data — the strongest set of consumer data rights in the US.

laws.title: California's Banking Regulations and Fintech Innovation
laws.subtitle: California hosts the largest concentration of fintech companies and has progressive banking rules
laws.fullDescription: California is home to Silicon Valley's fintech boom and has developed regulatory frameworks to balance innovation with consumer protection. The California Department of Financial Protection and Innovation (DFPI) regulates banks, credit unions, and new fintech lenders. California passed the Digital Financial Assets Law (2023) creating a licensing regime for cryptocurrency businesses. California's Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) requirements push banks to lend in underserved communities. California has strict payday lending limits and consumer protection rules far exceeding federal minimums. Bank of America, Wells Fargo, and Charles Schwab are headquartered in California.
laws.penalty: DFPI can revoke licenses and impose fines; crypto businesses without Digital Financial Assets licenses face civil penalties
exceptions: Federally chartered banks are primarily regulated at the federal level

quiz.q: What did California's Digital Financial Assets Law (2023) create for cryptocurrency businesses?
options: A licensing regime for crypto businesses
quiz.explanation: California's Digital Financial Assets Law (2023) created a mandatory licensing regime for cryptocurrency businesses operating in California — the most comprehensive state crypto regulation in the US, designed to protect consumers while providing regulatory clarity for the industry.

laws.title: California Retail Food Code & Proposition 65 Food Warnings
laws.subtitle: California mandates strict food safety and cancer-risk warnings on food products
laws.fullDescription: California's Sherman Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Law and the California Retail Food Code set strict standards for food handling, labeling, and facility inspections. But uniquely, Proposition 65 (Safe Drinking Water and Toxic Enforcement Act of 1986) requires businesses to provide 'clear and reasonable' warnings before knowingly exposing anyone to chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm — including many that occur in food (acrylamide in fried foods, lead in some dietary supplements). California also requires country-of-origin labeling for certain foods and has led the US in banning specific food additives (brominated vegetable oil, potassium bromate, red dye 3, titanium dioxide) that remain legal federally.
laws.penalty: Proposition 65 violations: civil penalties up to $2,500 per day per violation; food facility violations: fines up to $1,000 per day plus closure orders; false labeling: criminal misdemeanor
exceptions: Businesses with fewer than 10 employees are exempt from Prop 65 warning requirements
Naturally occurring chemicals in food have different exposure thresholds
Federal USDA-inspected facilities may have some federal preemption

quiz.q: What does California's Proposition 65 require food businesses to provide regarding certain chemicals?
options: Clear warnings before exposing consumers to chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm
Country of origin labeling for all ingredients
Daily temperature logs for refrigerated items
quiz.explanation: California's Proposition 65 requires businesses to provide clear warnings when products or facilities expose people to chemicals on the state's list of known carcinogens or reproductive toxins — including chemicals that naturally occur in some foods.

laws.title: California Animal Cruelty and Pet Store Ban
laws.subtitle: Strongest state-level animal protection laws in the US
laws.fullDescription: California has landmark animal welfare legislation. AB 485 (2017) banned pet stores from selling dogs, cats, and rabbits from commercial breeders, requiring stores to source animals from shelters and rescues only. California Penal Code 597 criminalizes animal cruelty with felony charges for intentional abuse. The state also bans foie gras production (forced-feed duck/goose livers), circuses using exotic animals, and the sale of most fur products (AB 44, 2019). California led the US in these protections — the fur ban made it the first US state to prohibit fur product sales.
laws.penalty: Animal cruelty misdemeanor: up to 1 year jail and $20,000 fine; felony cruelty: up to 3 years state prison; pet store violations: $500 per animal per day
exceptions: Livestock and agricultural practices have separate exemptions
Hunting and fishing governed by separate Fish and Game Code
Medical/scientific research facilities under USDA oversight

quiz.q: What did California's AB 485 require of pet stores regarding dogs, cats, and rabbits?
options: They can only sell animals from shelters or rescues
quiz.explanation: AB 485 (2017) banned California pet stores from selling commercially bred dogs, cats, and rabbits — they may only offer animals sourced from shelters and rescue organizations.

laws.title: California Community Property and No-Fault Divorce
laws.subtitle: California's 50/50 marital asset split and easy divorce access
laws.fullDescription: California is a community property state — all assets and debts acquired during marriage are owned equally (50/50) by both spouses, regardless of who earned them. California was a pioneer in no-fault divorce, adopting irreconcilable differences as sufficient grounds in 1969 — the first US state to do so. This ended the need to prove adultery, abandonment, or abuse to get divorced. The 6-month waiting period applies from the date of filing. California also has domestic partnership laws giving registered domestic partners most rights of married spouses. Child custody decisions must prioritize the 'best interests of the child.' California's Family Code is comprehensive and frequently updated.
laws.penalty: Not applicable (civil family law); contempt of court: fines and up to 5 days imprisonment for violating court orders; non-payment of support: wage garnishment and licence suspension
exceptions: Separate property (pre-marital, gifts, inheritance) retains individual ownership
Post-nuptial and prenuptial agreements can modify property division
Transmuted property through legal agreement

quiz.q: What pioneering divorce law change did California adopt in 1969?
options: California became the first US state to allow no-fault divorce — irreconcilable differences only
California required mandatory marriage counseling before divorce
quiz.explanation: California became the first US state to adopt no-fault divorce in 1969, allowing couples to divorce simply by citing irreconcilable differences — eliminating the requirement to prove fault (adultery, abuse, abandonment). This California innovation spread nationally and is now the standard across all US states.

laws.title: California Homeowner's Bill of Rights
laws.subtitle: Anti-foreclosure & tenant protections
laws.fullDescription: California's Homeowner's Bill of Rights (AB 278/SB 900, 2013) prohibits dual-track foreclosure, requires a single point of contact for distressed homeowners, and mandates verification of documents before foreclosure. Proposition 19 (2020) reformed property tax inheritance rules. The state also has one of the nation's strongest tenant protection laws under AB 1482, capping annual rent increases at 5% + local CPI.
laws.penalty: Civil penalties up to $50,000 per violation for mortgage servicers; wrongful foreclosure subject to punitive damages
exceptions: Primary residences only
Certain small landlords exempt from AB 1482

quiz.q: What does California's AB 1482 cap annual rent increases at?
quiz.explanation: AB 1482 (Tenant Protection Act of 2019) caps rent increases at 5% plus the local Consumer Price Index, protecting tenants in most multi-family housing built before 2005.

laws.title: California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA)
laws.subtitle: Nation-leading data privacy and consumer rights law
laws.fullDescription: California's Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA, 2018, strengthened by CPRA 2020) gives consumers rights to know what personal data businesses collect, request deletion, opt out of data sales, and correct inaccurate information. It applies to businesses with over $25M revenue, 50,000+ consumer records, or deriving 50%+ revenue from selling data. The California Department of Justice and Privacy Protection Agency enforce it. Statutory damages range from $100-$750 per consumer per incident for data breaches. CCPA was the model for privacy laws enacted in over 15 other states. California also has the Consumer Legal Remedies Act (CLRA) prohibiting 24 specific deceptive practices.
laws.penalty: Data breach: $100-$750 statutory damages per consumer; intentional violation: up to $7,500 civil penalty per violation
exceptions: Applies to businesses meeting revenue/data volume thresholds
Right to opt out of sale of personal information
laws.source: Cal. Civ. Code §§ 1798.100 et seq. (CCPA/CPRA); CLRA

quiz.q: What minimum statutory damages can California consumers claim per incident under the CCPA for a data breach?
quiz.explanation: The CCPA provides statutory damages of $100 to $750 per consumer per incident (or actual damages if greater) for data breaches resulting from a business's failure to implement reasonable security measures — a significant per-person figure given the scale of large breaches.

laws.title: Assault Weapon Ban — AWCA (1989)
laws.subtitle: California Assault Weapons Control Act — strictest in US
laws.fullDescription: California's Assault Weapons Control Act (AWCA) bans assault weapons defined by features: pistol grips, folding stocks, grenade launchers on semi-automatic centerfire rifles. The state maintains a registry of grandfathered assault weapons. The law has been repeatedly challenged but largely upheld. California also bans magazines over 10 rounds. Numerous court battles continue as federal courts issue conflicting rulings.
laws.penalty: Possession of unregistered assault weapon: felony, up to 1 year county jail or 16 months-3 years state prison.
exceptions: Pre-ban registered assault weapons (grandfathered)
Law enforcement and military exempt
Antique firearms pre-dating ban may qualify for exemption

quiz.q: What defines an 'assault weapon' under California's AWCA?
options: Any rifle capable of semi-automatic fire
Rifles with features like pistol grips or folding stocks
Any firearm with a detachable magazine
All firearms with more than 5-round capacity
quiz.explanation: California's AWCA defines assault weapons by features such as pistol grips, folding stocks, thumbhole stocks, and grenade launcher mounts on semi-automatic centerfire rifles. The feature-based definition has been central to ongoing legal challenges.

laws.title: CEQA — Environmental Quality Act
laws.subtitle: California Environmental Quality Act — most stringent state review
laws.fullDescription: California's Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) requires state and local agencies to identify and mitigate significant environmental impacts of proposed projects. Any project with potential environmental impact requires an Environmental Impact Report (EIR). CEQA has been used to block or delay housing, transit, and infrastructure projects. Reform efforts led to CEQA exemptions for infill housing near transit. California's environmental review process is often cited as a barrier to housing construction.
laws.penalty: Failure to complete required EIR: project injunction, contract void. Violations: civil fines up to $25,000.
exceptions: Ministerial projects exempt (no discretionary judgment required)
Categorical exemptions for small/routine projects
Infill exemption for housing near transit per SB 375/AB 2011

quiz.q: What is CEQA's primary requirement for major development projects in California?
options: Completion of an Environmental Impact Report
Planting trees equal to removed vegetation
quiz.explanation: CEQA requires completion of an Environmental Impact Report (EIR) for projects with potentially significant environmental impacts. The EIR must identify impacts and propose mitigation measures. CEQA review is often cited as contributing to California's housing shortage by enabling litigation to delay projects.

laws.title: AB 5 — Gig Worker Classification
laws.subtitle: Assembly Bill 5 (2019) — ABC test for independent contractors
laws.fullDescription: California's AB 5 (2019) codified the 'ABC test' for classifying workers as independent contractors. To be classified as independent, a worker must be: (A) free from control, (B) doing work outside the hiring entity's usual business, and (C) independently established in that trade. This affected Uber, Lyft, DoorDash, and gig economy platforms. Proposition 22 (2020) exempted app-based ride-share and delivery companies, but courts challenged the exemption.
laws.penalty: Worker misclassification: back wages, benefits, tax penalties, civil fines up to $25,000 per violation.
exceptions: Licensed professionals (doctors, lawyers, architects) have different tests
Prop 22 exempted app-based ride/delivery platforms
Over 100 occupational categories have specific exemptions

quiz.q: What is the 'B' prong of California AB 5's ABC test for independent contractor classification?
options: Worker is free from behavioral control
Work is outside the hiring entity's usual course of business
Worker has an independently established business
quiz.explanation: The 'B' prong requires that the work performed is outside the usual course of the hiring entity's business. This is often the most difficult prong for gig companies to satisfy — a driver working for a rideshare company is performing the core business of that company.

laws.title: Proposition 13 — Property Tax Cap
laws.subtitle: Prop 13 (1978) — 1% cap, 2% annual increase limit
laws.fullDescription: California's Proposition 13 (1978) amended the state constitution to limit property taxes to 1% of assessed value at purchase, with increases capped at 2% annually regardless of market appreciation. Properties are only reassessed upon sale. This created inequities between longtime owners (low taxes) and new buyers (higher taxes). It also significantly reduced school funding, requiring state equalization payments. Proposition 19 (2020) modified inheritance provisions.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties — Prop 13 is a tax limitation, not a criminal law. Non-compliance by government assessors is an administrative violation.
exceptions: New construction triggers reassessment
Change of ownership triggers reassessment
Prop 19 limits parent-child transfers to primary residences under $1M gain

quiz.q: Under California's Proposition 13, at what rate is residential property taxed?
quiz.explanation: Prop 13 limits property taxes to 1% of the property's assessed value at time of purchase, with annual increases capped at 2%. This means longtime homeowners often pay much lower taxes than new buyers of equivalent properties.

laws.title: Three Strikes Law — PC §667
laws.subtitle: Penal Code §667 — 25 years to life for third felony
laws.fullDescription: California's Three Strikes law (Penal Code §667, 1994) mandated 25 years to life for defendants convicted of a third felony, even if non-violent. California voters passed Proposition 36 in 2012, reforming the law so the third strike must be a serious/violent felony (with exceptions for certain crimes). The reform reduced the prison population and allowed resentencing for thousands already serving under the original law. California's prison system has been under federal oversight for overcrowding.
laws.penalty: Third serious/violent felony: 25 years to life. Second serious/violent felony: double the sentence.
exceptions: Prop 36 (2012): third strike must be serious/violent felony
Prosecutors may seek 25-to-life for non-violent third strikes with violent prior
Juvenile adjudications may count as strikes

quiz.q: What did California's Proposition 36 (2012) change about the Three Strikes law?
options: It abolished the Three Strikes law entirely
It required the third strike to be a serious or violent felony
It reduced the mandatory sentence to 10 years
It expanded Three Strikes to include misdemeanors
quiz.explanation: Proposition 36 (2012) reformed California's Three Strikes law to require the third strike to be a serious or violent felony. The original 1994 law allowed non-violent felonies as the third strike. Prop 36 also allowed resentencing for thousands already serving 25-to-life under the original law.

laws.title: Water Rights — Prior Appropriation vs. Riparian
laws.subtitle: California dual water rights system
laws.fullDescription: California has a complex dual water rights system combining prior appropriation (first in time, first in right) for most water and riparian rights (for landowners adjacent to water). The State Water Resources Control Board (SWRCB) administers water rights. During droughts, junior appropriators lose water access first. The Sustainable Groundwater Management Act (SGMA, 2014) created local agencies to manage groundwater sustainably by 2040. Water rights are a major source of litigation.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized water diversion: civil fines up to $1,000/day. Continuing violations: $500-$5,000/day. SWRCB may issue cease orders.
exceptions: De minimis water use exempt from diversion reporting
Pre-1914 rights are senior under prior appropriation
Riparian rights tied to land ownership (cannot be sold separately)
laws.sourceLabel: California State Water Resources Control Board

quiz.q: What did California's Sustainable Groundwater Management Act (SGMA, 2014) require?
options: Immediate end to all groundwater pumping
Local agencies to achieve groundwater sustainability by 2040
Federal oversight of all California water rights
quiz.explanation: SGMA (2014) required local agencies in California's high and medium priority groundwater basins to develop Groundwater Sustainability Plans and achieve sustainability by 2040. Prior to SGMA, groundwater was largely unregulated in California.

laws.title: Lane Splitting — Legal for Motorcycles
laws.subtitle: CVC §21658.1 — legal motorcycle lane splitting
laws.fullDescription: California is the only US state where motorcycle lane splitting (riding between lanes of traffic) is explicitly legal. Vehicle Code §21658.1 (2016) legalized lane splitting and directed CHP to develop safety guidelines. CHP recommends not exceeding 10 mph above traffic speed and not lane splitting above 30 mph. Lane splitting reduces motorcycle rear-end collisions in slow traffic. Studies show it can reduce congestion when widely practiced.
laws.penalty: No violation for compliant lane splitting. Dangerous lane splitting may be cited under unsafe operation provisions.
exceptions: No speed cap in the statute itself — CHP guidelines are advisory
Motorcycles with sidecars may not lane split
Lane filtering (stopped traffic) covered under different provisions

quiz.q: California is unique among US states for which motorcycle law?
options: Banning motorcycle helmet requirements for adults
Requiring motorcycle insurance at triple normal rates
quiz.explanation: California is the only US state where motorcycle lane splitting is explicitly legal under Vehicle Code §21658.1. CHP guidelines recommend not exceeding 10 mph above surrounding traffic and not lane splitting above 30 mph.

laws.title: AB 32 — Global Warming Solutions Act (2006)
laws.subtitle: First state economy-wide greenhouse gas law
laws.fullDescription: California's AB 32 (2006) required reducing greenhouse gas emissions to 1990 levels by 2020, making California the first jurisdiction to enact an economy-wide GHG cap. AB 32 created California's cap-and-trade program (launched 2013), linking with Quebec. California exceeded the 2020 target early. SB 32 (2016) extended the target to 40% below 1990 levels by 2030. California's climate laws have influenced federal and international policy.
laws.penalty: Cap-and-trade violations: allowance surrender penalties, financial penalties. Uncovered emissions: $43+ per ton CO2e.
exceptions: Small businesses under threshold may be exempt from cap-and-trade
Agricultural operations have modified requirements
Some industries receive free allowances in early compliance periods

quiz.q: What was California's greenhouse gas reduction target under the original AB 32?
quiz.explanation: California's AB 32 required reducing GHG emissions to 1990 levels by 2020. California exceeded this target early, and SB 32 (2016) extended the ambition to 40% below 1990 levels by 2030.

laws.title: SB 1437 — Felony Murder Reform
laws.subtitle: Senate Bill 1437 (2018) — limiting felony murder liability
laws.fullDescription: California's SB 1437 (2018) significantly reformed felony murder rule liability. Under the old rule, anyone participating in a felony resulting in death could be convicted of murder even without intent to kill. SB 1437 limits murder liability to: actual killers, those who aided with intent to kill, and major participants who acted with reckless indifference to human life. The law allowed thousands of prisoners to petition for resentencing.
laws.penalty: Murder: 25 years to life or life without parole for first degree. Resentencing petitions evaluated individually.
exceptions: Police officers killed in course of duty still subject to broader liability
Certain enumerated felonies (kidnapping, arson) have specific murder provisions
SB 775 (2021) extended resentencing provisions further

quiz.q: What did California's SB 1437 change about the felony murder rule?
options: It eliminated the felony murder rule entirely
It limited liability to actual killers and those with intent to kill
It expanded felony murder to include misdemeanors
It increased penalties for all murder convictions
quiz.explanation: SB 1437 limited felony murder liability to actual killers, those who aided with intent to kill, and major participants who acted with reckless indifference. Previously, any participant in a felony resulting in death could be convicted of murder regardless of intent.

laws.title: Tenant Protections — AB 1482 Rent Cap
laws.subtitle: Assembly Bill 1482 (2019) — statewide 5%+CPI rent cap
laws.fullDescription: California's AB 1482 (2019) implemented the first statewide rent cap: annual increases limited to 5% plus local CPI (max 10%). It also requires just cause for evictions after 12 months of tenancy. The law exempts single-family homes (unless owned by corporations), condos, and buildings built within the last 15 years. Many cities have stricter local rent control. Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act (1995) limits local rent control to units built before 1995.
laws.penalty: Illegal rent increase: tenant may seek rent repayment, relocation assistance. Bad-faith eviction: damages up to 3x monthly rent.
exceptions: Buildings built within 15 years exempt from AB 1482
Single-family homes (non-corporate owner) exempt
Properties with affordable housing agreements exempt

quiz.q: What is California AB 1482's formula for the maximum annual rent increase?
options: Equal to the federal minimum wage increase
quiz.explanation: AB 1482 caps annual rent increases at 5% plus local CPI, with a maximum of 10%. This applies to covered multifamily housing after 12 months of tenancy. Many cities like San Francisco and Los Angeles have stricter local rent control ordinances.

laws.title: Proposition 65 — Chemical Disclosure
laws.subtitle: Safe Drinking Water and Toxic Enforcement Act (1986)
laws.fullDescription: California's Proposition 65 requires businesses to provide 'clear and reasonable' warnings before knowingly exposing anyone to chemicals on the state's list of known carcinogens or reproductive toxins (over 900 chemicals). The ubiquitous 'California Prop 65 Warning' signs appear on buildings, products, and websites. Critics argue the warnings have become so common they lose meaning. Proposition 65 also prohibits businesses from discharging listed chemicals into drinking water sources.
laws.penalty: Violating Prop 65 warning requirement: civil penalty up to $2,500 per day per violation. Private enforcement (bounty hunter) suits are common.
exceptions: Exposures at or below 'safe harbor' levels exempt
Naturally occurring chemicals in food exempt
Specific exemptions for certain occupational exposures

quiz.q: How many chemicals are on California's Proposition 65 warning list?
quiz.explanation: California's Proposition 65 list contains over 900 chemicals known to cause cancer, birth defects, or other reproductive harm. Businesses must provide warnings before exposing people to these chemicals above safe harbor levels.

laws.title: Medi-Cal — Expanded Medicaid
laws.subtitle: California's universal low-income health insurance
laws.fullDescription: California's Medi-Cal (Medicaid) covers about 15 million Californians — the largest state Medicaid program. California expanded Medi-Cal under the ACA to cover adults up to 138% of the federal poverty level. In 2024, California expanded Medi-Cal to all income-eligible undocumented immigrants regardless of age — the first state to do so. Medi-Cal covers most healthcare services including dental, mental health, and substance use treatment.
laws.penalty: No penalty for individuals — enrollment is voluntary. Providers who commit Medi-Cal fraud face criminal prosecution, fines, and exclusion.
exceptions: Income and residency requirements apply
Emergency Medi-Cal available to all California residents regardless of documentation
Some services require prior authorization

quiz.q: What made California's 2024 Medi-Cal expansion historically unique?
options: It was the first state to expand Medicaid above 200% poverty level
It covered all income-eligible undocumented immigrants of all ages
It provided free dental care to all residents
It eliminated all co-payments for low-income enrollees
quiz.explanation: In 2024, California became the first state to expand Medi-Cal (Medicaid) to all income-eligible undocumented immigrants regardless of age. Previous expansions had covered undocumented children and then adults up to 49, but full expansion to all ages was unprecedented.

laws.title: Minimum Wage — $16/Hour (2024) + $20 Fast Food
laws.subtitle: California leads nation with sector-specific minimums
laws.fullDescription: California's minimum wage reached $16/hour statewide in 2024, the highest general minimum wage among large states. AB 1228 (2023) established a separate $20/hour minimum for fast food workers (chains with 60+ locations) effective April 2024 — the highest sector minimum in US history. Healthcare workers received a minimum wage increase to $18-23/hour depending on setting under SB 525. Local jurisdictions including Los Angeles ($17.28) and San Francisco ($18.67) have higher minimums.
laws.penalty: Minimum wage violations: back pay plus liquidated damages (double the underpayment), civil penalties $100-$250/violation.
exceptions: Learner rate allows $11.00/hour for first 160 hours
Agriculture workers have separate schedules
Youth employment certificates allow $11 for students

quiz.q: What minimum wage did California's AB 1228 establish for fast food workers at chains with 60+ locations?
quiz.explanation: California's AB 1228 (2023) established a $20/hour minimum wage for fast food workers at chains with 60 or more locations, effective April 2024. This is the highest sector-specific minimum wage in US history and applies to major chains like McDonald's, Starbucks, and Chipotle.

laws.title: CCPA — Consumer Privacy Law
laws.subtitle: California Consumer Privacy Act (2018) — strongest US privacy law
laws.fullDescription: The California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA, 2018) gives California residents the right to know what personal data businesses collect, the right to delete their data, the right to opt-out of data sales, and the right to non-discrimination for exercising privacy rights. CPRA (2020) expanded protections and created the California Privacy Protection Agency (CPPA). CCPA applies to businesses with $25M+ revenue or handling 50,000+ consumers' data. It has influenced privacy legislation nationally.
laws.penalty: Intentional violation: civil penalty up to $7,500 per record. Unintentional: up to $2,500. Data breaches: $100-$750 per consumer per incident.
exceptions: B2B transactions have limited exemptions
Employment data has modified requirements
Small businesses (under $25M revenue) generally exempt

quiz.q: What is the civil penalty for an intentional violation of California's CCPA per consumer record?
quiz.explanation: California's CCPA allows civil penalties of up to $7,500 per record for intentional violations and $2,500 for unintentional violations. Additionally, consumers may seek $100-$750 per incident for data breaches under the private right of action provision.

laws.title: SB 54 — Sanctuary State Law
laws.subtitle: California Values Act (2017) — limits cooperation with ICE
laws.fullDescription: California's SB 54 (California Values Act, 2017) limits state and local law enforcement cooperation with federal immigration enforcement. Law enforcement agencies are prohibited from using resources to investigate, detain, or arrest for immigration purposes; from inquiring about immigration status; and from honoring civil ICE detainer requests (only criminal detainer warrants permitted). The law was challenged but upheld by federal courts. California also enacted AB 32 (2019) banning private immigration detention facilities.
laws.penalty: Law enforcement agencies face no direct penalty, but individuals harmed by violations may sue. Agency non-compliance investigated by AG.
exceptions: Law enforcement may notify ICE of individuals convicted of certain serious/violent felonies
Court orders (not just detainers) must be honored
Secure Communities information sharing requirements remain federal

quiz.q: Under California's SB 54, when may local law enforcement cooperate with ICE detainer requests?
options: Never — all ICE detainers are prohibited
Only when supported by a judicial warrant
For any undocumented immigrant regardless of crime
quiz.explanation: SB 54 allows law enforcement to honor ICE detainer requests only when supported by a judicial warrant (court order), not civil administrative detainers. California may also notify ICE of individuals convicted of certain serious/violent felonies.

laws.title: Rooftop Solar — NEM 3.0
laws.subtitle: Net Metering 3.0 (2023) — reduced solar export credits
laws.fullDescription: California has the nation's most solar panels per capita. Net Energy Metering (NEM) allowed rooftop solar owners to sell excess electricity to utilities at retail rates. NEM 3.0 (2023) reduced the export credit rate by ~75% for new solar customers (to ~$0.05/kWh vs. retail ~$0.30/kWh) while increasing incentives for battery storage. The change was controversial — solar industry argued it would slow adoption; utilities argued old rates unfairly shifted costs to non-solar customers.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties for solar installation. Utility disconnection for non-compliance with interconnection rules.
exceptions: Existing NEM 1.0/2.0 customers grandfathered for 20 years
Low-income customers have modified 'NEM Equity' tariff
Community solar subscribers have different rate structures

quiz.q: By approximately how much did California's NEM 3.0 reduce the export credit rate for new rooftop solar customers?
quiz.explanation: California's NEM 3.0 (2023) reduced the solar export credit rate by approximately 75% for new customers — from about $0.30/kWh (retail rate) to about $0.05/kWh. The change was intended to encourage battery storage pairing but was criticized by the solar industry as harming adoption.

laws.title: Worker's Compensation — Presumption Laws
laws.subtitle: California workers' comp covers all injuries
laws.fullDescription: California's workers' compensation system covers all employees (including undocumented workers) for work-related injuries and illnesses. Employers must carry workers' comp insurance or be self-insured. California has strong presumption laws for public safety workers: firefighters and police officers are presumed to have work-related cancer, heart disease, and certain other conditions. The exclusive remedy doctrine generally bars lawsuits against employers for covered injuries.
laws.penalty: Employer without workers' comp insurance: stop-work order, $10,000+ fines, personal liability for claims. Premium fraud: criminal felony.
exceptions: Sole proprietors and partners may opt out
Domestic workers working under 52 hours/quarter exempt
Out-of-state employers with California employees have special requirements

quiz.q: Are undocumented workers covered by California's workers' compensation system?
options: No — only legal residents are covered
Yes — all employees including undocumented workers are covered
Only for injuries in specified industries
Only if the employer opts into undocumented worker coverage
quiz.explanation: California's workers' compensation system explicitly covers all employees regardless of immigration status. Undocumented workers injured on the job are entitled to medical treatment and disability benefits equal to those of legally authorized workers.

laws.title: Zero-Emission Vehicle Mandate — CARB 2035
laws.subtitle: California bans new gas car sales by 2035
laws.fullDescription: California's Advanced Clean Cars II rule (2022) requires all new passenger cars and trucks sold in California to be zero-emission by 2035. This is the first such mandate in the US. Plug-in hybrids may account for up to 20% of sales. The rule applies to model year 2026+ vehicles with escalating ZEV percentages. 17 other states have adopted California's ZEV standards. The federal Clean Air Act gives California unique waiver authority to set stricter vehicle emissions standards.
laws.penalty: Automakers selling non-compliant vehicles: civil fines. Dealers selling non-compliant new vehicles after 2035: violations subject to CARB enforcement.
exceptions: Used vehicles unaffected — used gas cars remain legal to own and operate indefinitely
Emergency vehicles may have modified timelines
Certain specialty vehicles have longer compliance timelines
laws.sourceLabel: California CARB — Advanced Clean Cars II

quiz.q: Under California's 2035 zero-emission vehicle mandate, what percentage of new car sales may be plug-in hybrids?
quiz.explanation: California's Advanced Clean Cars II rule requires all new passenger vehicles to be zero-emission by 2035, but allows plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs) to account for up to 20% of new sales. The remaining 80%+ must be fully battery-electric or hydrogen fuel cell vehicles.

laws.title: LGBTQ+ Protections — FEHA Coverage
laws.subtitle: Fair Employment and Housing Act — comprehensive protections
laws.fullDescription: California's Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity, and gender expression in employment, housing, and public accommodations. California was among the first states to prohibit LGBT workplace discrimination (1999). AB 196 (2022) requires businesses with 50+ employees to have gender-neutral single-occupancy restrooms. SB 396 (2017) requires employers to provide harassment prevention training covering gender identity. California bans conversion therapy for minors.
laws.penalty: FEHA violations: administrative complaints, civil damages, attorney's fees. Conversion therapy on minors: professional license revocation, civil liability.
exceptions: Religious organizations may have BFOQ defense for employment of co-religionists
Small employers (under 5) exempt from FEHA employment provisions
Reasonable accommodation requirements balance privacy interests

quiz.q: California's AB 196 (2022) required which specific change to commercial facilities?
options: Addition of all-gender restrooms to all businesses
Gender-neutral signage on single-occupancy restrooms for businesses with 50+ employees
Transgender-only restroom facilities in public buildings
Gender-neutral restrooms in all new construction
quiz.explanation: AB 196 (2022) requires businesses with 50 or more employees to designate single-occupancy restrooms as all-gender/gender-neutral. The law covers single-occupancy facilities that can only be occupied by one person at a time.

laws.title: California Constitution — Unique Provisions
laws.subtitle: 6th most-amended US state constitution
laws.fullDescription: California's constitution is unusually detailed and frequently amended by voter initiative. Key unique provisions: Proposition 98 (1988) guarantees K-14 education approximately 40% of state general fund revenue; Article 34 requires voter approval for public housing projects; strong privacy right in Article 1 §1 (added 1972) interpreted broadly by courts. California voters can initiate constitutional amendments with 8% signature threshold. The constitution has been amended over 500 times since 1879.
laws.penalty: Constitutional violations subject to judicial review and invalidation; officials violating constitutional provisions face civil/criminal liability.
exceptions: Some provisions apply only to state government, not private actors
Federal supremacy limits state constitutional provisions
Emergency provisions allow temporary suspensions of some requirements

quiz.q: What does California's Proposition 98 (1988) guarantee regarding education funding?
options: Approximately 40% of the state general fund for K-14 education
Equal per-pupil spending across all districts
Federal matching funds for California schools
quiz.explanation: Proposition 98 (1988) constitutionally guarantees that K-14 education (K-12 public schools and community colleges) receives approximately 40% of California's state general fund revenues. This 'minimum guarantee' has become the baseline for education budget negotiations.
